->*lord.*<-

**W**hile I was considering a patron, by whose protection and authority this distinguished treatise on the Philosophical work <note>original: "opere Philosophico." In this context, "philosophical" refers to alchemy and the study of natural secrets.</note> and the highest Medicine might be fortified, and thus fortified might venture more safely into the public eye, I could find no protection more suitable or certain than yours, O Most Noble and Distinguished Man. For the fame and renown of your name arises from your supreme services toward this our fatherland, to whose well-being <note>original: "saluti," meaning both health and general welfare.</note> not only by your art...

# TO THE
## SINCERE READER.

I thought it worthwhile, *Sincere Reader* <note>original: "Lector Candide," a traditional Latin greeting to the "fair-minded" or "honest" reader, implying the author hopes for an unbiased reception.</note>, to inform you of the reasoning behind my undertaking. And in the first place, why I wished this book to be published with such a title prefixed to it. Indeed, I have no doubt that to many it seems too pompous and arrogant; but he who will not find it a burden to run through the whole <term>little book</term> <note>original: "libellum," a modest term for a shorter treatise or volume.</note> with both mind and eyes will discover that here the names match their subjects. For what wonders do not reveal themselves in the making of the *Philosophers’ Stone* <note>original: "Lapide Philosophico," the legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold and providing an elixir of life.</note>, in *particular transmutations* <note>The process of changing one substance or metal into another.</note>, in *philosophical salts*, in *extracts*, in *distilled waters*, and so forth? What *medical mysteries* are not found in the final part of this little work? Read first, therefore, and understand; then judge, and not before. To be sure, I am not unaware that for a master of this art <note>The "art" referred to here is alchemy, often called the "Hermetic Art" or "Spagyric Art" during this period.</note>, there are neither miracles nor mysteries. For so it is in every art, even the most abstruse: nothing is strange or rare to the expert. But let these things pass. Wherefore

<summary>In this preface, Valckenier defends the potentially "pompous" title of his book by arguing that the wonders of alchemy and medicine contained within—such as the Philosophers' Stone—justify his bold language.</summary>
<keywords>alchemical wonders, Philosophers' Stone, transmutations, medical mysteries, distilled waters, 17th-century chemistry, preface to the reader</keywords>

### To the most Distinguished & excellent Man,

# LORD DR. PHILIPP MÜLLER,
## most skilled <term>Chymiatrist</term>. <note>original: "Chymiatro," a practitioner of iatrochemistry, a branch of medicine popularized by Paracelsus that used chemical and mineral substances as treatments.</note>

### Hearty Greetings. <note>original: "S. P." for "Salutem Plurimam," a standard Latin epistolary greeting.</note>

## CASPAR BARTHOLIN
### *The Dane, Doctor of Philosophy & Medicine.*

So, I hear at last that you are about to publish, my dearest <note>original: "oculissime," literally "most eye-like," a term of endearment for a friend as precious as one's own eyes.</note> **Müller**, the monuments of your genius, which have been hidden long enough until now. You will think, I know well, that they are being brought into the light in due time. But no one else besides you thinks so <note>A friendly nudge suggesting that Müller’s colleagues have been waiting impatiently for this work.</note>. Since we were once joined in conversation in **Italy**, that queen of regions, I refresh your memory of what you promised: namely, that you would not delay in the publication, because of the subject of the work, which is for the public good. Come then, keep your word! To me, indeed, [give] your love; since it is not permitted in body, in spirit [I am joined] to you...

<meta>catchword: joined</meta>

<summary>Caspar Bartholin writes to Philipp Müller, urging him to fulfill a promise made in Italy to publish his chemical-medical works for the public benefit. Bartholin praises Müller's intellect and notes that the academic community has long awaited these writings.</summary>
<keywords>Caspar Bartholin, Philipp Müller, iatrochemistry, Italy, medical publishing, public good, 17th-century medicine</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory letter from Caspar Bartholin to Philipp Müller. Bartholin is reinforcing their bond of friendship and urging Müller to overcome his fear of critics and publish his work, citing the biblical parable of the talents.</meta>

I am joined, by that best part of me <note>That is, joined in spirit or soul.</note>. Ensure that the covenant of friendship entered into between us dies only with us. As for me—so may our holy **Hygeia** <note>The Greek goddess of health and hygiene, often invoked by physicians of this era.</note> love me—I promise you this affection: which (I swear by the spirit of **Friendship**) has been intense toward you from the moment I conceived it. Indeed, because it is for the sake of virtue, which is eternal, I shall nourish it eternally; although also because of your reciprocal love for me, by which you value and esteem me more than my mediocrity deserves.

Keep your word, I say, and publish those <term>Chemical</term> <note>original: "Chymica," referring to the early modern study of chemistry and alchemy.</note> wonders of yours. Publish them: lest you seem to have buried in the ground the **talent** <note>A reference to the biblical Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25), where a servant is punished for hiding his money/skills instead of using them for profit.</note> entrusted to you by God. Do you fear the attempts of certain noisy critics to overwhelm your budding **Fame**? Laugh, laugh in return, and free yourself from them by mere contempt, as you are doing. Rather, consider it a stroke of luck. For the more a tree has flourished into many branches, the thicker the noise it makes when moved by a violent breeze <note>The OCR reads "arcâ," likely a transcription error for "aurâ" (breeze/wind) given the context of a tree rustling.</note>; but more strongly, than...

<summary>Bartholin encourages Müller to publish his chemical research, warning him not to "bury his talent" due to fear of critics. He uses the metaphor of a flourishing tree to explain that success naturally attracts more noise and attention.</summary>
<keywords>friendship, Hygeia, chemistry, Parable of the Talents, academic rivalry, Caspar Bartholin, Philipp Müller</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues the metaphor of a tree to describe the nature of public reputation. Bartholin is encouraging Müller to remain steadfast against critics, arguing that the "storms" of envy are actually proof of a person's growing success and virtue.</meta>

<sig>* 6</sig>
<meta>catchword: various,</meta>

than another tree equipped with fewer branches, it resists: In the same way **Fame**, **Virtue**, and **Learning** <note>original: "Fama, Virtus, Eruditio." In this context, "Virtus" refers to moral excellence or skill, and "Eruditio" to scholarly knowledge.</note> increase and multiply the further they expand; yet for that very reason, they are more heavily pressed, disturbed, and tossed about by the storm of the envious and the whirlwind of the malevolent. However, they are not crushed, not driven out, and not swept away.

For that reason, you should rather desire even a commotion of heaven and earth against you, as an infallible sign of more substantial virtue and more widespread **Fame**. Meanwhile, seek **Fame** as if you were going to despise it; and despise it as if you were going to seek it. Just as by traveling through the world we learn to despise the world, so by anxiously seeking the flattering breeze of **Fame**, we learn to regard it as nothing more than a breeze, a shadow, a void. In the meantime, through this contempt for **Fame** and **Glory**, we run—whether we like it or not—into the reward of these very things, even if it was not sought after.

Do you wish to know about me, and on what hinge <note>original: "quo versentur in cardine," a Latin idiom meaning the "turning point" or the current state of affairs.</note> your friend's affairs are turning? Here is the news in brief. My **Medical** works <note>original: "Medica," referring to Bartholin's prolific output in anatomy and medicine.</note> are currently boiling under my hands <note>This is an idiom meaning he is working intensely and rapidly on his manuscripts.</note>...

<summary>Bartholin uses the metaphor of a sturdy tree to explain that criticism and envy are natural signs of a growing reputation. He advises his friend to remain indifferent to fame while reporting that he is currently busy finishing his own medical writings.</summary>
<keywords>Fame, Virtue, Envy, Resilience, Medical writings, Caspar Bartholin, Stoicism</keywords>

...various works, which are eager to come out; and among them leading the way: several hundreds <note>original: "Centuriæ aliquot." In early modern scholarship, a "Century" was a common way to organize a collection of one hundred observations, paradoxes, or medical cases.</note> of **Philosophical and Medical Paradoxes**; some small **Anatomical** works; a **Treatise on Cauteries** <note>original: "de Cauteriis." Cautery involved using heat or caustic chemicals to sear tissue, treat wounds, or stop bleeding.</note>; a **Book on Opium and Opiate Laudanums** <note>original: "de Opio & Laudanis Opiatis Liber." Opiate "laudanums" were various medicinal preparations of opium used as painkillers and sedatives.</note>, etc. Would that they be for some public good! Indeed, I try more than I achieve; I wish, as much as I am able, to be of benefit to the public. I profess this openly. Yet results do not entirely fail every effort, nor does the power to act fail every will.

**As for you, let me know more clearly what you are doing now, and especially how your health is: and remain toward me as you have shown yourself to be; be certain that from Bartholin <note>The author, Thomas Bartholin (1616–1680), here refers to himself in the third person, a common formal convention in Latin correspondence of this period.</note> the same loyalty will be yours: Greetings from my heart; I who desire the best for you from my heart: and greet your father, a most distinguished senator <note>original: "senatorem amplissimum." Likely referring to a member of a high-ranking city council or administrative body.</note>, and no small lover and investigator of nature <note>original: "indagatorem." This implies a person who actively researches or observes the natural world, similar to a "naturalist."</note>, on my behalf.**

<summary>Thomas Bartholin lists his forthcoming medical and anatomical publications and concludes his letter with warm wishes for Müller's health and a respectful greeting to Müller's father.</summary>

# PHILIP MULLER'S
### OF FREIBURG,
### DOCTOR OF PHILOSOPHY AND MEDICINE.
# BOOK I.
## *On the Philosopher's Stone.*
## PREFACE.

I approach the Subject Matter <note>original: "materiam"; referring to the physical substance or "First Matter" used to create the Philosopher's Stone</note>, with God's blessing, which has been celebrated for so many centuries and even now is daily praised; yet it is rare in actual practice, and encountered by very few; not indeed because of its difficulty, since it is "work for womenfolk" <note>original: "opus muliercularum"; a common alchemical phrase suggesting that once the secret is known, the labor is as simple as household chores like cooking or washing</note>; but because of the obscurity of the authors and their tangled manner of writing; who, so that they might cloud anything in this art, leave nothing untried. And in this regard, all the moderns <term>neoterici</term> <note>referring to "new" or contemporary alchemical writers of the 16th and 17th centuries</note> err much more than any of the ancients, who always used a clearer style of speech in explaining this mystery of nature: so that, unless the more recent writers had continually shrouded it more and more in darkness, many more would have reached the desired goal before long. Nor have they only zealously pursued obscurity; but...

<meta>catchword: etiam</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Philip Muller introduces his treatise on the Philosopher's Stone, arguing that the art is inherently simple but has been intentionally obscured by modern authors' confusing writing styles.</summary>
<keywords>Philip Muller, Alchemy, Philosopher's Stone, Preface, Ancients vs Moderns, Materia, Mystery of Nature</keywords>

## PREFACE

...they have even used an inverted and preposterous order of speaking; so that what ought to be the first step in the work, some have assigned to the very last place. Some have even mixed in the most foreign matters, which have no more to do with this mystery than Aesop’s fables. From all these vices I shall certainly strive to be as free as possible and as is permitted—not as if I have personal experience in this divine and rare work (for I would not dare to aspire to that), but as one who will set forth more clearly and in the best order those things which others, both ancient and modern, have produced in a most disordered and obscure fashion. 

And in truth, it would have been better for those who publish writings on this subject almost every year—incomplete and obscure as they are—to have remained entirely silent, rather than causing a waste of time and money for both themselves and others. 

Therefore, I will bring to public light something I do not know to have been attempted before me. I do so not from what I have gained through experience (for I have candidly confessed my lack of this before, and I do not deny it now), but rather whatever truth I have been able to grasp through the scrutiny of reason from the published books of both recent and ancient authors; whatever I have been able to draw from very ancient manuscripts seen in Germany and Italy; and finally, whatever I have studied and perceived from the conversations of the most learned men and friends. I shall provide exact figures of the *Philosophic tower* <note>original: "turris Philosophicæ"; a specialized alchemical furnace, also known as an Athanor, designed to maintain steady heat over long periods</note> for everyone; then, I will treat the *matter of the Stone* <note>original: "materia Lapidis"; the "First Matter" or base substance required to begin the alchemical transformation</note>, as far as it has been possible to understand it; and finally, its *preparation*, from—

<meta>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword "solu-" suggests the next word is "solution" or "absolute."</meta>

<summary>Muller critiques the disorganized and misleading nature of contemporary alchemical literature and proposes a new, orderly synthesis based on extensive research of manuscripts and expert consultations.</summary>

# P R E F A C E .

...which seem to look toward the resolution and perfection <note>original: "solutionem & perfectionem"</note>; so that for one who has the leisure and the mind for this matter, a not difficult access to these secrets may lie open. And in treating all these things, I will set aside the judgment of all those who laugh falsely at everything said about the **Philosopher's Stone** <term>Philosopher's Stone: The legendary substance sought by alchemists, believed to be capable of turning base metals into gold and acting as an elixir of life.</term>, as if such things were false, trifling, and impossible. If I wanted to mutter even a single word against them, I would surely be as completely insane as they are.

Is that Stone perhaps fictitious because **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and **Aristotle** <note>These are the traditional authorities of ancient medicine and philosophy whose works dominated European thought for centuries.</note> do not hand it down? O, how many things are known today that were never known to them! Nor is there a lack of countless authors, great men—some more ancient than them, some more recent—who possessed the best knowledge of this matter. 

They think one species cannot be **transmuted** <term>transmutation: The process of changing one substance or element into another, the core goal of alchemy.</term> into another. O, what raving ignorance! They distrust their own eyes, which see infinite things always changing into others, and one thing always being made from another. They even distrust their seeing eyes and hearing ears regarding the true gold made through art in various places (I do not say *natural* gold, as some unskilfully babble, since what is made by art is *artificial*)—gold that is excellent and pure, withstanding all tests. 

If you desire to see this, travel through the Christian world, or at least the parts and regions of the world near to you. If you always stick to your mother soil, turn your eyes through **Barnaud's** booklet *On Christa* <note>original: "Barnaudi de Christa libellum." This refers to Nicolas Barnaud, a 16th-century physician and alchemist; the "Christa" likely refers to his work on the "Aelia Laelia Crispis" enigma.</note>, which names the first experiences—

# PREFACE.

...filled with very true citations <note>The Latin text begins with the suffix "-tim," likely completing a word like "testimoniis" (testimonies) from the previous page.</note>. But I cease to speak further on this matter, because among truly learned and true Philosophers, these things have never been placed in doubt. Nevertheless, these things had to be introduced for the sake of beginners, who are forced to believe and defend what their more ignorant masters—who are sworn to **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus was a 2nd-century physician whose works were the absolute authority in medicine for centuries. The author is criticizing "Galenists" who refuse to look at new chemical evidence.</note> as if to a sole **GOD**—dictate, and who know nothing beyond the wisdom of those masters. So unhappy are these times, in which modern <term>Doctors</term> <note>From the Latin 'Doctores,' meaning university-educated scholars or teachers.</note> do not wish for their students to become superior to themselves; indeed, they forbid it. In these times, I say, the students themselves do not think of anything more sublime, nor do they search their minds for anything beyond what they have learned from their teachers. The common crowd repeats one thing: "Where are those goldsmiths and <term>Alchemists</term> <note>The author is addressing the public's skepticism: if alchemy is real, why aren't alchemists visibly wealthy?</note>? Why do they not show everyone that they possess the art, so that they might be more easily believed? Nowhere in any region do such men appear who are known to live off it, much less grow rich from it."

->To which I respond<-

that it is most correctly said: *It is not known*. For indeed, can one who finds a precious treasure be of such small mind that he would show and reveal it to those from whom he is certain that danger, disgrace, and slander would then threaten him? Thus, most unhappy are those who, while others are ignorant, know this art of making the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the 'Great Work' of alchemy.</note>. Now kings and princes, like bird-catchers, demand it from them, either through great promises of obtaining favor and honor, or through threats, imprisonment, and torture...

# PREFACE.

...death. If you are free from these dangers, at the very least you will be exposed to the mockery of the common crowd, and today you will hear the name of **Alchemist** <term>Alchemist</term> <note>In this period, "Alchemist" was often used as a slur for counterfeiters or "puffers" who wasted money on failed experiments, as opposed to "Chemists" or "Philosophers."</note> spoken of as something hated beyond measure. For which reason, I swear by Hercules <note>The Latin *herclè* is a common emphatic oath.</note>, I would never desire to actually hold the manual practice of this operation in the **Secret Stone** <term>Secret Stone</term> <note>Latin: *Lapide arcani*. This refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the "Great Work" in alchemy, believed to possess transmutative and curative powers.</note>. But no one shall ever forbid me from contemplating in my mind those things which are wonderful in nature—mysteries which were granted to be considered not by brute beasts, but by man alone. Therefore, having set aside all other matters, I hasten to the subject at hand.

## Concerning Mercury <note>original: ☿</note>.

**U**p to this point, it has been explained in general that a triple material is required for that celebrated Stone <note>The Philosophers' Stone, the legendary substance alchemists sought to create for transmutation and healing.</note>. First, we encounter that Hermaphrodite <note>Alchemists called Mercury an "Hermaphrodite" because they believed it possessed dual qualities—being both a liquid and a metal, or containing both "male" (hot/dry) and "female" (cold/moist) principles.</note>, namely Mercury. ## CHAPTER FOUR.
## On the Preparation & Purification of <term>Mercury</term>.

**T**ake now that <term>mercury</term>, and purge it diligently by straining it several times through a clean, triple-folded linen cloth, until it appears as pure as the clearest crystalline water. We reject those purifications made with vinegar, salt, urine, quicklime, <term>vitriol</term> <note>A sulfate mineral, often used as a corrosive in early chemistry.</note>, and other corrosives: which destroy the moisture of the <term>mercury</term> rather than elevating it; and thus they cause more loss than gain.

## CHAPTER FIVE.
## On <term>Silver</term> and <term>Gold</term>, and Their Preparation.

**T**he other Matter of the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosophers' Stone, the goal of the Great Work.</note>, which is called the "female," follows: <term>silver</term>. It should be sought in its purest state from the mines, not worn out by any previous uses, not having experienced too much fire, and not mixed with foreign things. Let it be easily malleable; in short, the best that can be had of its kind. Let it be drawn into very thin leaves or plates, though others may reduce it to a <term>calx</term> <note>original: "calcem". A powder produced by heating a metal to remove its "moisture" or to oxidize it.</note>. And consider the same to be said of <term>gold</term>: that it be of a saturated color as much as possible, ductile, and most pure. For as you sow, so shall you reap. <note>original: "Nam ut sementem feceris, ita et metes." A proverbial warning that the quality of the final "harvest" or alchemical result depends entirely on the purity of the initial ingredients.</note>

# C H A P T E R  S I X.
## *On the Work Itself.*

**W**e have emphasized up to this point those things which must precede the <term>Work</term> <note>original: "opus". In alchemy, "The Work" refers to the specific laboratory process of creating the Philosophers' Stone.</note> itself, before the craftsman girds himself for labor. We will now approach the Work itself, which everyone desires most greedily; and what others have taught quite obscurely, we shall bring forth more clearly into the light: and hereafter the sense of the words will not be difficult during the operation. This, however, must be noted above all: that in the operation for the <term>white</term> or the <term>red</term> <note>original: "album vel rubrum". These are the two final stages of the process: the White Work produces silver (or the Little Elixir), while the Red Work produces gold (or the Great Elixir).</note>, distinct <term>Matter</term> <note>original: "materiam". The starting chemical substance.</note> must be used; but the operation is the same. Therefore, what is said here about the operation for the white should also be understood as applying to the one that tends toward the red.

First, however, we must speak of the <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrefactione". The stage where the material decomposes and turns black, often called the "Nigredo."</note> of the Matter, which is followed thereafter by <term>resuscitation</term> <note>original: "resuscitatio". The process of bringing the "dead" or decomposed matter back to life in a purified state.</note> and <term>exaltation</term> <note>original: "exaltatio". An operation by which a substance is raised to a higher dignity or more potent medicinal virtue.</note>. Neither can these latter stages emerge unless the former has preceded them. For indeed, the generation of one thing is the corruption of another, and vice versa; any seed cast into the earth, of whatever herb it may be, first putrefies over a period of time and loses its form: once this is done, a new power which previously lay hidden and concealed exerts itself as the celestial heat <note>Typically refers to the heat of the sun, or a laboratory fire designed to mimic the sun's natural warmth.</note> approaches; and the third part containing the seed, moistened by dew and rain, serves as a promotion so that the putrefied seed might rise up into another, more excellent and noble body,

...may bear fruit and manifold offspring. This is the character of nature, even in all animals; they are first nourished and grow gradually, and finally they intend generation at the proper time, once their commanded growth has been reached. If this is true in humans, animals, and plants—as indeed no one but those who are willfully blind can fail to see—why should this same thing not be so in minerals, at least by analogy? 

You might say that in animals the logic is different, since the seed of two is required for any offspring: a male and a female. But I answer that in man, two bodies contain the seed, which later constitute a single seed; in minerals, one substance performs this alone. And why not? Does not the seed also proceed from a single source in plants? For that masculine or feminine sex attributed to plants <note>The author refers to the early botanical understanding of plant reproduction, which was often described using gendered metaphors before modern genetics.</note>, whether for "mutual love" or some other property, does not actually contribute anything to the production of its like. But lest we overstep the bounds of our purpose by wandering too widely, we now approach our work.

...are given to the body, either 2 or 4 parts of the <term>menstruum</term> <note>original: "menstrui." ## PART TWO
### OF THE WORK.

**N**ow take all the <term>water of life</term> <note>original: "aquam vitæ." This refers to a distilled solvent, often alcohol or a potent acid, believed to carry the "life force" of the substance.</note>, and put it into vials sealed in the same way as before, in the same ashes, and with the same degree of fire—namely, the first degree <note>The "first degree" of fire refers to the lowest heat, comparable to the warmth of a brooding hen.</note>. Put this water back in, and proceed in this way until no more of the skin or blackness appears.

# PART THREE.

**A**ll of the <term>Raven’s Head</term> <note>original: "Caput Corvi." This is the black substance resulting from the putrefaction of the material, a necessary first step in the "Great Work."</note> collected from there is placed in the <term>Philosophical Egg</term> <note>original: "ovo Philosophico." An egg-shaped glass vessel used by alchemists to simulate the natural environment of gestation and growth.</note> depicted above, and set in oak ashes. These are heated to the first degree of heat <note>The "first degree" is a gentle warmth, similar to the heat of the sun in spring or a brooding hen.</note> using well-burnt, smokeless coals of any kind. Let the mouth of the neck be hermetically sealed. [Seal] the middle with a moderate paste, so that it can always be easily opened. For the first eight days, more or less, because the black and dead earth is still "drunk" <note>original: "ebria." Alchemists often described saturated materials as "drunk" and dry materials as "thirsty."</note>, let it finish without further drink. Afterward, when it is dried out and "thirsty," let it be given a "drink" of the <term>water of life</term> <note>original: "aquâ vitæ." A distilled solvent or spirit used to nourish the matter.</note>—specifically, an equal portion of it—with the glass open. Mix it well, then close it. Leave it in this state, not until it is completely dry, but until the whole is well clotted together into one mass. With the glass opened again, proceed in the same way as before, until the matter has soaked up all the water.

# PART FOUR.

**N**ow let this matter be placed into the "egg" in the second degree of fire <note>A stronger heat than the first, used to drive the transformation further.</note>; and let it be left for several months until at last it turns into a **white color** <note>original: "colorem album." This stage is known as the "albedo," representing the purification and "resurrection" of the matter after its "death" in the black stage.</note>. Meanwhile, however, a variety of many colors will present themselves to be seen <note>This colorful transition is often called the "Peacock's Tail" (cauda pavonis) in alchemical literature.</note>.

# M I R A C L E S

## P A R T  F I V E .

**N**ow the <term>whitened earth</term> <note>original: "terra dealbata." This refers to the matter after it has reached the "albedo" or white stage of the process.</note> is ready, and in its next potential state to receive the seed, due to the fertility acquired through its cultivation. Take this and, once weighed, divide it into three parts, so that the weight of the remaining components may be known. Now take one part of <term>ferment</term> <note>original: "fermenti." A substance added to the "stone" to finalize its transformation, acting like yeast in dough.</note>, equal in weight to one of the three parts already weighed. Take 4 parts of the <term>harlot’s menstruum</term> <note>original: "menstrui mulieris meretricis." In alchemy, "menstruum" refers to a solvent. The "harlot" is a metaphorical term for a substance—often mercury or a specific corrosive—that easily combines with many different metals.</note>. Let an amalgam be made of the laminated ferment, as described above, and the menstruum; and let a solution be made in a <term>vial</term> <note>original: "phiala." A glass vessel with a long neck.</note> using gentle heat for 14 days, until the "body" is reduced into a fine <term>calx</term> <note>original: "calcem." A powder produced by heating or "calcining" a substance until it loses its moisture and structure.</note>. For here, <term>water of life</term> <note>original: "Aqua vitæ." A high-strength distilled spirit or solvent used as a reagent.</note> is not required. Now take the menstruum with the calx of the body; and with all three parts of the whitened earth, let an amalgam be made on a marble slab. Put this into a glass vessel. Govern the fire at the second degree <note>A moderate heat, stronger than a brooding hen but not yet boiling.</note> for a month. Finally, let the heat of the third degree <note>A strong heat, often using a sand bath to distribute the temperature.</note> be applied for as long as it takes until the matter is thoroughly whitened, becoming like a thick and hard mass, similar to pumice, but heavy. And thus far concerning the operation for the **white** <note>original: "ad album." The creation of the White Stone, which can transmute base metals into silver.</note>. For the **red** <note>original: "ad rubrum." The creation of the Red Stone or Elixir, the final goal, capable of making gold.</note>, the operation is no different, except that it is longer at the end, where the third-degree fire must be maintained longer than for the white; just as the red surpasses and excels the white in nobility. In the same way, when a magnificent house is built, it requires a longer time than a meager hut.

# PART SIX.

## **On the Preparation of the Stone already completed for Projection.**

<note>Decorative initial L</note>Many have possessed the completed <term>Stone</term> <note>original: "Lapidem." The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work.</note> without recognizing it, and without being skilled in the method of preparing it for <term>Projection</term> <note>original: "Projectionem." The final stage of alchemy where the "Stone" is cast upon base metals to transmute them into gold or silver.</note>. For the Stone thus finished will effect nothing in <term>Transmutation</term> unless it is made fit for the <term>ingression</term> <note>original: "ingressum." The ability of the alchemical medicine to "enter" or penetrate the pores of a solid metal to change its nature.</note> of bodies. Therefore, even when all things are rightly performed, unless this completion is added, the Labor has been undertaken in vain. Wherefore, grind your stone into pieces and place it in an <term>egg</term> <note>original: "ovo." The "philosophical egg" was a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck, symbolizing a womb where the Stone is matured.</note>, the bottom of which—all the way up to the neck—should be covered everywhere with good <term>lute</term> <note>original: "luto." A protective paste made of clay, dung, or hair, used to seal vessels and protect them from shattering in high heat.</note>, so that it can withstand a strong fire, nearly of the <term>fourth degree</term> <note>The "fourth degree" was the most intense heat in the alchemical laboratory, often compared to the heat of a melting furnace or glowing coals.</note>. For this reason, the second part of the <term>philosophical furnace</term> <note>A specialized furnace (sometimes called an Athanor) designed to provide consistent, controlled heat over long periods.</note> must now be removed; and fire must be applied in the first part, or larger furnace, from below, where the grate is located, just as previously in the second part. In place of ashes, let <term>sand</term> be used <note>A "sand bath" (balneum arenae) provides a more intense and even heat than an ash bath.</note>. Let a strong fire of coals be urged until the sand is so hot that it gives off a hissing sound upon the drop of a drop of water, and the touch cannot endure the heat of the protruding neck. Let it stand thus until it becomes a fine and very light powder; which usually happens in the space of a month or a month and a half.

# PART SEVEN,
# AND LAST.

## *On the Augmentation or Multiplication of the Stone.*

**<note>Decorative initial L</note>L**apidem <note>original: "Lapidem." The Philosopher's Stone.</note> you can multiply the acquired Stone infinitely, so that it is not necessary to so often repeat the very tedious labor of [creating] the whole Stone. Therefore, of the Stone already completed in the fifth part of the operation, take one half for use and the preparation for projection, and keep the other half for multiplication. Weigh this half. And if there are three parts of this, take one part of the <term>water of life</term> <note>original: "aquæ vitæ." In alchemy, this usually refers to highly distilled spirit of wine (ethanol), used here as a revitalizing agent for the "Stone," though the author specifically warns not to confuse it with the "menstruum" or solvent used earlier.</note> (not the menstruum), so that there are 4 parts in total. Place this in an <term>egg</term> <note>original: "ovo." The "philosophical egg," a glass flask with a round body and long neck, used to simulate the conditions of a womb.</note> at a fire of the second degree for a month, and afterward at a fire of the third degree until the end, just as we taught in the fifth part of the operation.

And thus we have explained this most rare <term>Craft</term> <note>original: "Artificium." Referring to the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note>—which is rarely handed down correctly by others, and for the most part is certainly set forth in a backwards and inverted way, or else in a mutilated and imperfect fashion—clearly enough and in an orderly manner. If anyone pursues this path, leaving behind the trifles and nonsense of other impostors, there is no reason he should begin to despair of obtaining his goal. If anyone does not sufficiently understand these words of ours, let him [read them] once and again

## OF FREIBURG
## DOCTOR OF PHILOSOPHY & MEDICINE
### BOOK II.
### *Concerning Particular Transmutations.*

**H**aving laid out the **Universal** path <note>The "Universal path" refers to the creation of the Philosopher's Stone, which was believed to cure all diseases and transmute all metals.</note>, which anyone can safely follow, we shall also provide other **particular** methods to be used by those who wish to spare themselves expense, time, and labor. However, it must not be thought that such a "particular" path, or the treasure produced by it, can have any use in medicine, in the same way that the substance described and prepared in the previous book possesses incredible utility in healing the human body. For indeed, common and "leperous" <term>mercury</term> <note>original: ☿ (the symbol for Mercury). Muller calls it "leperous" because, in alchemical theory, base metals were considered "diseased" versions of gold.</note> contains within itself a supreme toxicity, which is not stripped away even when they apply the "hermaphrodite of the woman" to it <note>This is a coded alchemical reference to a reagent or process intended to "fix" or stabilize the mercury. The "woman" often represents the passive or material principle, while "hermaphrodite" refers to a substance sharing two natures, often a salt or a treated mineral.</note>; so that it is a marvel that some allow themselves such audacity and recklessness as to treat such things as the highest secrets and myste-

...mysteries to others, and they do not blush to win the favor of noblemen <note>original: "magnatum"</note> for themselves through them; even though they did not obtain these secrets through their own talent, but bought them at the highest price. In the <term>Mercury</term> of the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the respected alchemical authorities of antiquity and the Middle Ages.</note>, which is rightly called "doubled" by <term>Bernard, Count of Trevisan</term> <note>A famous 15th-century alchemist whose writings focused on the "Mercury of the Philosophers" as the key to the Stone.</note>; because after the physical body is cast off, one part is afterward joined to the other, and it resists poison like an <term>antidote</term> <note>original: "alexipharmacum," a term for a medicine that wards off poison.</note>. Those that proceed otherwise should be rejected, as they are marked with the crime of falsehood.

## THE FIRST METHOD

**T**ake 8 or 10 parts of our white vinegar <note>original: "aceti albi nostri"</note>. Of the finest salt and of our mother <note>In alchemy, the "mother" usually refers to the base mineral or primary substance from which the work begins.</note>, take 1 part each. Use the coagulated matter as you did previously; add the second part of the vinegar for the second time; and repeat this a third time, until it has consumed <note>original: "devoraverit"</note> the third and final part of the vinegar in the same way, and has stood again for a month. These things being done, take out your material and grind it upon the marble, and into the—

Transfer all of this matter into the oval <term>vial</term> <note>original: "phialam" — a glass laboratory flask.</note> depicted above, so that the bottom part, or one third, is filled; but let two parts remain empty. Let fire be applied in the first degree for the first month, in the second degree for the second month, and in the third degree for the third month. The fourth degree, for <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixationis" — the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note>, lasts for several weeks. The sign of fixation is an ash-gray color of the powder which is seen all around the matter. 

Now pour out the matter, which is already <term>coagulated</term> <note>original: "coagulatam" — turned from a liquid or powder into a solid mass.</note>, and you will have it. Here, as was noted above in the third degree, the "rising of the mountains" etc. present themselves to be seen, and they reveal the wondrous miracles of nature. In this work, the following furnace will be suitable.

**N**ow we are no longer inclined to mutter a single word against those who utterly despise all medicines derived from minerals, as if they possessed no compatibility with human nature. <note>Muller is addressing a major 17th-century debate between traditional Galenic doctors, who used only plants, and "iatrochemists" like himself, who used chemical and mineral substances.</note> Instead, we refer them to the most ancient authors, who utilized minerals even in their raw state for various diseases and circumstances, and not without success. We, however, shall expect even greater results from those minerals that have been rightly and legitimately prepared; such success has already been abundantly proven by infinite experiences. Indeed, when remedies made from plants—being milder—offer little help, we flee to medicines of this kind as if to a <term>sacred anchor<gloss>sacram anchoram</gloss></term>. <note>The "sacred anchor" was a common Latin idiom for a last resort or a final, most reliable hope in a crisis.</note>

Let them, therefore, cease to object to the incompatibility of minerals with the human body, and to extol their own remedies from plants above all others. For what is more compatible with the human body than the human body itself; from whose various parts we know how to prepare the most noble medicines. <note>In the 17th century, substances like "mummy" or powdered human skull were actually used in pharmacy, a practice known as medical cannibalism or "corpse medicine."</note> Meanwhile, it can be unknown to no one how rarely, timidly, and fearfully some physicians today use these. Furthermore, medicines taken from animals are certainly closer to human nature than those derived from plants. Although they do indeed use these, it is not to the same extent as they use plants. Therefore, let this be established: God has given us medicines from every kind of living thing—from man himself, from brute animals, from plants, and from minerals and metals—which I, for my part, believe to be alive. <note>Muller adheres to the vitalist view common among iatrochemists, believing that minerals and metals possess a "life" or spiritual essence that can be extracted for healing.</note> Now we shall direct our discourse to the matter at hand.

## CHAPTER ONE.

### *On Preparations from <term>Mercury</term>.* <note>original symbol: ☿</note>

### I. *Preparation of <term>Mercury</term>.*

**T**ake 6 <term>ounces</term> <note>original symbol: ℥</note> of refined mercury. <note>original: "mercurii meteorisati," referring to mercury that has been purified, likely by distillation or "raised" to a higher state.</note> 4 and a half <term>ounces</term> of the *best properly purified water.* Mix in a mortar until all the water is consumed by the earth. <note>In early chemistry, "earth" refers to the solid base or the powdered substance being worked upon.</note> Let a sublimation be made in a long-necked matrass <note>A glass vessel with a round bottom and a long neck used for distillation and sublimation.</note>, over a <term>fire</term> <note>original symbol: △</note> of the third order <note>Early chemists categorized fire intensity by four degrees; the "third order" refers to a strong heat, such as a hot sand bath.</note>, always discarding the material remaining at the bottom whenever the sublimation is repeated. Finally, reduce it to a fine powder <note>original: "alcohol," which in this period referred to any extremely fine, impalpable powder produced by grinding or sublimation, not liquid spirits.</note> and keep it for use. <term>Quercetanus</term> <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a famous French physician and champion of Paracelsian chemical medicine.</note> calls this preparation the <term>White Eagle</term> <note>original: "Aquilam albam"</note>: its use is remarkable in various diseases, such as incipient leprosy, <term>syphilis</term> <note>original: "lue ♀," using the astrological symbol for Venus to denote the "venereal disease."</note>, worms in children, dropsy, gout, etc. The dose is from 12 to 20 grains, taken with "cochia" pills <note>A common type of purgative pill.</note>, "aggregative" pills, or others. And then they call such pills those of <term>Quercetanus</term>. We were unwilling to keep this <term>secret remedy</term> <note>original: "arcanum"</note> hidden because of the great and notable use it can provide to the human race. Others call it "sweet sublimate." The most famous and distinguished chemist, Mr. Johann Friedrich Echsius, a physician of Rheinfelden, calls it <term>Sweet Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurium dulcem," known today as calomel (mercurous chloride), which was less toxic than other mercurials.</note>. Others call it the <term>Celestial Eagle</term> <note>original: "Aquilam cœlestem"</note>.

**T**ake refined <term>mercury</term> <note>original symbol: ☿; the Latin "meteorisato" suggests mercury that has been purified or "raised" through sublimation.</note> and <term>saturnine magnesia</term>. <note>A preparation of lead; "Saturn" is the alchemical name for lead.</note> Grind them, mix them, and place them in a <term>retort</term>. <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</note> With the <term>fire</term> <note>original symbol: △</note> increased by degrees, a gummy liquor will drip out; pour this over <term>cinnabar</term> <note>A bright red mineral, mercury sulfide.</note> made from mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note> and lead <note>original symbol: ♄</note> that is to be sublimated. The most happy success of this remedy has often been proven by experience. In this <term>arcanum</term> <note>A secret medicinal or alchemical preparation.</note>, the entire body of <term>gold</term> <note>original symbol: ☉</note> is dissolved; from which <term>leprosy</term> is most perfectly cured.

### Balsam of Mercury <term>☿</term>.

**I**t shall be reduced into a red and sweet powder; if it is first <term>coagulated</term> <note>Turned from a liquid or vapor into a solid state.</note> through water distilled from the whites of eggs cooked to hardness <note>hard-boiled egg whites</note>. # CHAPTER TWO.

## Concerning Preparations from <term>Antimony</term> <note>Original symbol: ♁. Antimony was one of the most important minerals in the alchemist's pharmacy, used both as a medicine and a key agent in refining other metals.</note>.

### I. The First and Best Preparation of <term>Antimony</term> <note>♁</note>.

**T**ake 8 <term>ounces</term> <note>Original: ℥</note> of pure <term>iron</term> <note>Original: Mars (♂). Iron was used to "purify" antimony by drawing away impurities.</note> plates and place them in a <term>crucible</term> <note>Original: †. A ceramic or metal container used for melting materials at very high temperatures.</note> at the bellows-furnace. When the iron glows white-hot, add 16 <term>ounces</term> <note>℥</note> of antimony <term>♁</term>. Let them melt under the most intense heat, and afterwards throw in 4 <term>ounces</term> <note>℥</note> of pure, refined <term>saltpeter</term> <note>Potassium nitrate, used here as a flux to help the metal flow and to oxidize impurities.</note>. Let the heat continue until the entire material flows like oil. Then you shall have ready a pyramidal cup <note>A conical mold used to allow the molten metal to settle into a point.</note> greased on the inside with wax; it should be well heated. Pour the flowing material from the furnace out of the <term>crucible</term> <note>†</note>. Once it has cooled, pour it out of the mold and knock off the upper <term>scoriae</term> <note>The dross or glassy waste material that floats to the top of the molten metal.</note>, and you will have the <term>Regulus</term> <note>The "Little King"—the pure metallic heart of the antimony that settles at the bottom of the mold, often forming a star-like pattern on its surface.</note>. Later, grind this Regulus with 3 <term>ounces</term> <note>℥</note> of fresh antimony <term>♁</term> in a new <term>crucible</term> <note>†</note>. Melt it and add 3 <term>ounces</term> <note>℥</note> of saltpeter just as you did before; while everything flows like **fire** <term>△</term>, pour it into the said cup and collect the yellow <term>scoriae</term>. Repeat this operation as many times as necessary, until the <term>Regulus</term> is entirely consumed into the <term>scoriae</term>. Keep this. It performs wonders for all those in need of <term>evacuation</term> <note>The medical practice of purging the body, typically through induced vomiting or bowel movements, believed to remove "corrupt humors" causing disease.</note>.

### **Sweet Oil of <term>Antimony</term> <note>Original symbol: ♁. Antimony was a cornerstone of "Iatrochemistry" (chemical medicine) in the 17th century.</note>, for human Medicine, the secret of secrets.**

**T**ake 2 pounds of powdered <term>antimony</term> <note>♁</note> and 3 pounds of *common salt*.
Grind them together on a preparatory stone. Melt them. Pour them out. Grind them again very finely. Wash <note>Original: Edulcora. To "sweeten" or "edulcorate" meant to wash away salts or acids with water until the substance was tasteless/pure.</note> with warm water; this labor must be repeated three times. Then dry the <term>antimony</term> <note>♁</note>, grind it again, and <term>sublime</term> <note>A process where a solid is heated until it turns into a vapor and then collects again as a solid in a cooler part of the vessel.</note> it by itself in a vessel for simple Flowers of Sulfur; then the excess spirits and sulfur will depart upward. To the residue remaining at the bottom, add *vinegar* and extract the color for as long as the *vinegar* is being tinted. Distill this through a filter and draw off the <term>menstruum</term> <note>A solvent; here, the vinegar used for extraction.</note> in a <term>Bain-Marie</term> <note>Original: B.M. A water bath used for gentle, steady heating.</note> until an oil-like substance appears at the bottom. Remove this from the <term>cucurbit</term> <note>The lower part of a distilling apparatus, shaped like a gourd.</note> and place it in a vial, then add the best circulated <term>Spirit of Wine</term> <note>Concentrated alcohol/ethanol.</note>. <term>Seal the vessel hermetically</term> <note>Original: S.H. (Sigillo Hermetico). To melt the glass neck of a flask shut to make it completely airtight.</note> perfectly. <term>Digest</term> <note>To keep a substance at a constant, gentle heat to encourage a chemical change.</note> in a <term>Bain-Marie</term> <note>B.M.</note> for one month. Then distill further. Finally, distill through a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass bulb with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids that require higher heat.</note>. First, the spirit will come forth. Then, however, the true Oil of <term>Antimony</term> <note>♁</note> will come, which is red and sweet, known to few.

This was shared with me by the most distinguished and excellent man, Lord Doctor Caspar Bartholin the Dane, Philosopher and Physician <note>Caspar Bartholin the Elder (1585–1629) was a famous Danish polymath and professor whose anatomical works were standard textbooks for decades.</note>.

Take 1 <term>drachm</term> <note>Original symbol: ʒ. A small unit of weight, about 3.9 grams.</note> each of **Antimony, Mastic, white Frankincense, and Myrrh**.
Powder them all and pour on the **Aqua Vitae**, and let them be placed for <term>digestion</term> <note>The process of steeping a substance in a solvent with gentle heat to extract its medicinal properties.</note> while well-sealed. Let them be distilled in an <term>ash bath</term> <note>A method of heating a vessel by surrounding it with hot ashes to ensure even, gentle temperature.</note> through an <term>alembic</term> <note>A traditional distilling apparatus consisting of two parts: a boiling pot and a cooling cap with a delivery tube.</note> according to the art. First, the **Spirit of Wine** <note>S.V. (Spiritus Vini).</note> rises with a slow fire, and it stinks. Once the stench is lost, it acquires a more pleasant odor. This oil thoroughly heals wounds that are difficult to cure.

## CHAPTER THREE.

### Concerning preparations from <term>vitriol</term> <note>A group of sulfate minerals; "Green vitriol" is iron(II) sulfate, while "Blue vitriol" is copper(II) sulfate. They were primary sources for sulfuric acid.</note>. I. The true <term>spirit of vitriol</term> <note>A volatile liquid distilled from vitriol; effectively a dilute form of sulfuric acid.</note>.

**T**ake **vitriol**, place it in an earthen <term>cucurbit</term> <note>A gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation.</note>, and put on the <term>cap</term> <note>Original: *capitellum*. The lid or alembic head of the still where vapors collect.</note>. Apply fire and increase it according to the rules of the art, until the entire vapor takes the form of a liquid. When you see it no longer distilling, increase the fire so strongly until white vapors come out. Continue until none appear. Thus the **vitriol** will be most perfectly **calcined** <note>Reduced to a dry, crumbly powder through the application of intense heat.</note>, and you will have the spirit in the <term>phlegm</term> <note>The watery, less potent part of a distillate.</note> in this way. Distill in a cucurbit, in a <term>Bain-Marie</term> <note>Original: *B. M.* (Balneum Mariae). A water bath used for gentle, uniform heating.</note> or a fire of ashes, until all the phlegm has gone out. The spirit will be left at the bottom. Let the calcined matter be put into a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</note>; distill in the usual manner and you will have **oil** and **spirit**. But for the spirit previously left at the bottom, so that it may be obtained without a foul smell and made most fragrant, do this: Take some of the <term>colcothar</term> <note>The reddish-brown residue (iron oxide) remaining after the distillation of vitriol.</note>, which you should soak with the spirit, and let it stand for a while. Afterwards, draw out the spirit from it with a very slow heat. Thus it will be most fragrant.

## III.

### *The Most Proven and Secret Oil of <term>Vitriol</term> <note>Though called an "oil" due to its thick consistency, this is concentrated sulfuric acid.</note>.*

**T**ake Hungarian <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: *Vitriolum Ungaricum*. This refers to blue vitriol or copper(II) sulfate, which was famously mined in the regions of Upper Hungary (modern-day Slovakia).</note> of a blue color, and reduce it into a <term>calx</term> <note>A dry powder produced by heating a substance to remove moisture.</note> with prepared flint stones. Pour over it circulated <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>High-proof distilled alcohol (ethanol).</note>, so that it slightly covers the solids. Then, separate the burning <term>fire</term> <note>The manuscript uses the Greek letter delta (Δ), the alchemical symbol for fire.</note> by distillation in a <term>retort</term> or a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>Distillation vessels; a retort has a long integrated neck, while a cucurbit is the base of a multi-part still.</note> tilted to the side. Having drawn this off gradually, urge the spirits by increasing the fire more and more until all the spirits have passed over. Place this distilled liquid into a <term>blind alembic</term> <note>original: *alembicum caecum*. A distillation head without a spout, used for "digesting" or circulating vapors back into the liquid rather than collecting them elsewhere.</note>, and <term>macerate</term> <note>Soak or soften.</note> it in a <term>Bain-Marie</term> <note>original: *B.M.* (Balneum Mariae). A gentle water bath.</note> for eight days. Take care that the water boils lightly, and only the <term>aquosity</term> <note>The watery, non-essential part of the mixture.</note> rises, while the oil remains at the bottom. To achieve and separate this, you will need three days of work. But if any wateriness remains mixed in, it is necessary that the <term>phlegm</term> <note>The weak, watery residue of distillation.</note> be separated again. Then you will receive a most sweet and red oil. This process of distilling Oil of Vitriol is the most proven and secret of all.

Place it in a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass distillation vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck.</note> coated with the best <term>lute</term> <note>A protective clay or paste used to seal joints and protect glass from direct flame.</note>, and let it be distilled just like <term>spirit of vitriol</term> <note>original: *sp. Vitr.* Sulfuric acid.</note>. Apply a slow fire for several hours, increasing it gradually until the spirit emerges in the form of a vapor, which will cloud the receiving vessel. It is used for all internal ailments, such as obstructions and the decaying of the internal organs; it wonderfully dissolves <term>calculus</term> <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note> and <term>gravel</term> <note>original: *aren.* (sand or grit in the urinary tract).</note>, etc. Externally, it is effective for ulcers.

## II.

### *Calcined white vitriolated <term>tartar</term>.* <note>original: *Tart. album vitriolatum calcinatum.* A chemical preparation where tartar (potassium bitartrate) is burned to an ash and then reacted with sulfuric acid.</note>

**T**ake calcined <term>tartar</term>; dissolve it in liquid, filter it, dry it, and repeat this three times. Take 1 [part] <note>original: *j.* The specific unit is likely an ounce or pound depending on the scale of the laboratory.</note> and place it in a <term>luted</term> <note>Coated with a protective clay or paste to prevent the glass from shattering under heat.</note> small <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original: *cucurbatula*. A gourd-shaped vessel used for heating and distillation.</note>. Pour on 4 or 5 ounces of rectified <term>oil of vitriol</term> <note>original: *oleum vitriol. rectif.* Concentrated sulfuric acid.</note>, but do so gradually, drop by drop; otherwise, the heat generated <note>original: *accensum*. In this way, the material is coagulated, and a white color immediately settles to the bottom. Then, pour off this floating oil of vitriol from the material at the bottom. Distill off the moisture in a <term>Mary’s bath</term> <note>original: *B. M.* (Balneum Mariae). A water bath used to provide gentle, consistent heat.</note>; thus you have fixed <term>tartar</term>. It purges from below <note>Acts as a laxative.</note> and through sweat <note>Acts as a diaphoretic, a common method in early medicine to expel "ill humors."</note>. It is effective for stubborn afflictions, <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: *hydropem*. Swelling caused by excess fluid in the body.</note>, <term>the stone</term> <note>original: *calculum*. Kidney or bladder stones.</note>, <term>gout</term> <note>original: *podagram*.</note>, plague, and <term>scurvy</term> <note>original: *scorbutum*.</note>. To purge from below, mix it with honey, rose syrup <note>original: *rosac.* (rosaceo).</note>, or another syrup. To induce sweating in cases of plague and dropsy, take it with <term>Blessed Thistle</term> water <note>original: *aqua card. bened.* (*Carduus benedictus*), a popular medicinal herb.</note>, <term>Scabious</term> water <note>original: *Scab.* (*Scabiosa*), used for skin and respiratory ailments.</note>, or with <term>theriac</term> <note>A famous ancient medical "cure-all" paste consisting of many ingredients, often used as an antidote.</note> made into pills. The dose is from half a <term>scruple</term> <note>An apothecary weight; half a scruple is roughly 0.6 grams.</note> to one full scruple.

# V.

## **The Secret of Tartar, for all malignant**
### **ulcers.**

**T**ake three pounds of <term>calcined tartar</term> <note>original: "Tartari calcinati." Tartar (potassium bitartrate) that has been heated to a high temperature until it becomes a white or grey ash.</note>. Moisten it with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original: "spiritu vini." Distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note> for seven days. Digest it in a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "B." or "Balneum Mariae." A vessel of water used to heat another container gently.</note>. Lastly, let all the collected black juices be <term>coagulated</term> <note>Solidified through evaporation.</note> into a powder. By moistening with <term>oil of vitriol</term> <note>original: "ol. vitriol." Concentrated sulfuric acid.</note> and spirit of wine, let the essence be thoroughly drawn off from the calcined tartar. **One grain** <note>approx. 65 milligrams</note> of this medicine, taken with **half a dram** <note>approx. 1.8 grams</note> of <term>mithridate</term> <note>original: "mithridatis." A complex semi-mystical polypharmaceutical or "universal antidote" used since antiquity.</note> in **chicory water**, according to the severity of the disease and the condition of the patient, fundamentally pulls out the root and origin of all <term>malignant ulcers</term> <note>original: "ulcera maligna." Severe, non-healing, or potentially cancerous sores.</note>.

# CHAPTER FIVE.

## On Preparations from Arsenic.

### I.

#### Preparation of Arsenic for cancerous, <term>scirrhous</term><note>Hard, slow-growing malignant tumors.</note>, malignant ulcers, <term>hypersarcomata</term><note>Fleshy overgrowths or "proud flesh" produced during wound healing.</note> etc.

**T**ake one pound of crystalline arsenic, three ounces of the best tartar, and one pound of <term>saltpeter</term><note>original: "salis nitri." Potassium nitrate, used here as an oxidizing agent.</note>; let them be ground separately and then mixed. Heat a large <term>crucible</term><note>original: "†." A ceramic or metal container used for melting materials at very high temperatures.</note> most intensely, and into it, while it is glowing hot, let the powder be thrown by the spoonful, covering it slightly with the spoon; it will melt immediately with a great deal of smoke. Leave it until it almost ceases to smoke. Then let it be poured into a marble mortar, or another vessel, and let it be allowed to cool. A reddish mass will be obtained, which should be mixed and ground with an equal weight of saltpeter; let this be done as above in the same or a new crucible. Let it be subjected to the fire for 6 hours; the material will become very white. When it has cooled, it must be thrown into hot water to separate the saltpeter and the tartar; at the bottom will remain <term>fixed arsenic</term><note>original: "Arsenicum fixum." In early chemistry, "fixing" a substance meant making it non-volatile or stable when heated, often believed to remove its poisonous qualities.</note>, corrected and freed from all poison. Let the washing be repeated often in a large quantity of water; let the fused material be thrown into the water immediately. The water containing the salts ought to be saved for washing, or the salt may be separated by evaporation for use.

# BY PHILIP MÜLLER
## OF FREIBURG,
### DOCTOR OF PHILOSOPHY & MEDICINE.
### BOOK IV.

*Concerning the more secret methods of producing extracts, distilled waters, balms, essences, and Philosophic salts, etc., from simple vegetables.* <note>In the 17th century, "vegetables" referred to all plant life, not just culinary vegetables. "Philosophic salts" are purified salts believed to contain the "body" or "earth" of the plant.</note>

Up to this point, we have taught those things which are produced from minerals, intended both for Transmutation <note>original: "Transmutationem." The alchemical process of changing base metals into gold or silver.</note> and for medicine. We have not covered every process, but rather the principal ones: for we have wished to observe this rule in our entire work—that we would publish nothing unless it were either very rare, highly useful, or a secret <note>original: "arcanum." A hidden or esoteric teaching or formula.</note> not previously disclosed in print. The rare items we have given so far; they are highly useful and, for the most part, were not previously published. 

Now, we shall not begrudge others those things which possess remarkable utility in Medicine, to be derived from <term>simples</term> <note>original: "simplicibus." Single medicinal herbs or plants used as the basis for remedies, as opposed to "compounds" which are mixtures.</note> of the plant kingdom. Nor shall we remain silent about those which have, until now, always been kept at home as secrets. And to begin, we will teach the method of making an extract from any "simple"—for example, from a root, wood, herb, seed, fruit, or flower, and so on. How useful this is to every physician and patient is something that everyone can see.

# CHAPTER ONE.

## Concerning the Method of making an Extract from any simple <note>original: "simplici." In historical medicine, a "simple" refers to a single medicinal herb or plant used on its own, rather than a "compound" of many ingredients.</note>.

**B**esides the instruments, you should have two materials ready at hand: The first is that simple substance from which you seek the extract. The second is the <term>Menstruum</term> <note>original: "Menstruum." A solvent used to dissolve a solid and extract its "virtue" or active medicinal properties.</note>, by which you will select out the virtue of that simple. In choosing this solvent, various people err in various ways; to review and refute all of these errors would be the task of a man with too much leisure. However, it is necessary to expose as erroneous a practice which most people have adopted as a custom: namely, that they commonly use <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original: "spiritum vini." High-proof alcohol or ethanol, usually distilled from wine.</note> for any and every purpose without discrimination. 

In this matter, they err for several reasons. First, if those simple things from which the extraction is to be made are quite delicate, then the more subtle part of the plant is released into the spirit of wine far too suddenly and aggressively. Then, and what is most important, since the spirit of wine is extremely "hot" in nature, it imbues the substance with an alien quality and infects it with a <insert>t</insert>artarous spirit <note>The text reads "artareo," likely a printer's error for "tartareo." In the chemistry of this period, "tartar" was associated with harshness, acidity, or the tendency to form stones/obstructions.</note>. Furthermore, spirit of wine is not found in such abundance in every part of the world, or if it is, it is certainly rarely of good quality; likewise, it must be purchased at a high price. For this reason, it is advantageous to choose such a menstruum which can be easily obtained everywhere in the world without cost, and which, on account of its temperate quality...

...an artificial <note>original: "artificialem." In this context, it refers to a process made by art or skill, rather than occurring naturally.</note> extraction. Remove it. A process of slow, gentle heating to further refine and combine the substances.</note> in a moderately warm and gently boiling <term>Mary's Bath</term> until it reaches the proper consistency that pleases you. 

Of this essence, well-preserved, if a little is put into wine, the wine will turn a deep red. Proceed thus in the extrac... <note>original catchword: "ctione." This is the end of the word "extractione."</note>

# CHAPTER TWO.

## *Concerning the Method of making Distilled Waters from simples, while retaining their color, scent, and flavor.*

**T**ake any herb (or flower, wood, etc., or any part of a plant), crush it, and pour over it three times the amount of its own <term>solvent</term> <note>original: "menstrui." In early chemistry, a menstruum was a solvent—such as water, wine, or vinegar—used to extract the medicinal or chemical properties of a substance.</note> or another of those mentioned. Place it in a pot with another pot placed on top; or, what is better, in a <term>cucurbit</term> with a <term>blind alembic</term>, ensuring all openings are sealed. Let them boil in ashes <note>An ash bath (balneum cinere) provided a steady, gentle heat, preventing the glass from shattering or the herbs from scorching.</note> until half the liquid is consumed, so that the material becomes somewhat thicker. This happens quite slowly, but the result is better for it. 

Afterward, remove the material and squeeze it out. Put the squeezed-out liquid into a narrow-necked <term>cucurbit</term> equipped with an <term>alembic</term> that has a base rising inward, as is drawn in the figures below <note>referring to the diagrams on the previous page</note>. Once the joints are sealed and the <term>cucurbit</term> is filled no more than halfway, place it in ash or sand. Proceed always from a gentler heat to a stronger one until the contents boil. 

Now the material will be seen to ascend by means of its <term>vapors</term> <note>original: "halitus," literally breath or exhalations.</note> and descend again like dew. Meanwhile, murmurs and noises will sometimes be heard, which occasionally happens when the vapors find a way to escape. Therefore, the craftsman must seal the joints thoroughly so that nothing escapes. This rising and falling of vapors shall continue so long

# WONDERS

## CHAPTER III.

*On the Method of making Balms from Simples.*

**W**e strive to write nothing that is commonplace or known to everyone; and thus, until now, we have provided methods known only to a few. There are also very few who are skilled in the true method of making <term>balms</term> <note>original: "Balsama." Fragrant, medicinal ointments or resins believed to have healing properties.</note> from <term>simples</term> <note>original: "simplicibus." In early medicine, "simples" were individual medicinal herbs or single ingredients, used on their own rather than in a complex mixture.</note>. It must be known from the start that a balm of any substance cannot be made unless the <term>oil</term> of that substance is first obtained, for the oil itself is the balm. The ways of making oils are varied; they are known everywhere and are described in all the books of the <term>chemists</term> <note>original: "Chymicorum." This refers to early modern practitioners of chemistry and alchemy.</note>. Therefore, we did not think it worth the effort to include them here. 

But if anyone wishes to obtain oil more quickly and abundantly from more expensive <term>aromatics</term> <note>original: "aromatibus." Spices, perfumes, or fragrant plant materials.</note>—specifically those that contain very little natural oiliness—let him take some of the golden-colored <term>May dew</term> <note>original: "rore majali." Dew collected in the early morning during the month of May. Early modern scientists and alchemists believed this dew was a "universal solvent" impregnated with celestial energy.</note> that can be found, provided it is pure and very sweet. With this dew, boil any crushed and broken herb or aromatic for a short time—about a quarter of an hour—until it has thoroughly soaked up the dew. Then, distill this impregnated material through a <term>retort</term> <note>original: "retortam." A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances by heating them and collecting the condensed vapor.</note>, and you will have an oil which, once <term>rectified</term> <note>original: "rectificatum." Purified or refined through a secondary distillation process.</note>, will be of the highest quality. Once the oil is acquired, others add wax and other substances to create a more suitable consistency—and indeed, to increase their profit <note>The author suggests that adding wax was often a way to "stretch" a small amount of expensive oil to sell more of it.</note>. I do not praise this common method, since in use ex-

[in]ternally or externally, the pores are closed up by the wax, so that the power of the balm cannot rightly penetrate; nor can it even be taken into the body. For this reason, we will share with others a way and method of making the best balms, so that they may be of use both internally and externally in the human body. And because everyone hides this method as if it were a great <term>arcanum</term> <note>original: "arcanum." A profound secret or a "closed" mystery, often used in alchemy to describe a powerful, hidden medicinal secret.</note>, we shall teach it. 

Some use the <term>axungia</term> <note>original: "axungiis." Soft animal fat or grease, often used as a base for ointments.</note> of various animals, such as the fat from the <term>caul of a kid</term> <note>original: "pinguedine omenti hœdini." The fatty membrane surrounding the internal organs of a young goat.</note>. Some make balms from honey, others from heavenly manna, by adding oil, as **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a famous French physician and chemist who championed the use of chemical medicines over traditional herbal ones.</note> does. 

We shall give a better way. Take 2 ounces of some oil; add 1 ounce of our <term>May dew</term> <note>original: "roris majalis." Dew collected in May, believed by early chemists to contain a celestial essence or "spirit of the world."</note>, previously well washed with the <term>simple water</term> <note>original: "aqua iſtius ſimplicis." Distilled water from the specific plant being used.</note> of the substance whose oil is being added. Let them be well incorporated together in a glass dish over a fire, so that the bottom is moderately heated. Let the mass cool; keep it for use. Used internally or externally, even the smallest amount of it is excellent. In this way, you will produce balms from the best materials without great expense, such as from cinnamon, cloves, etc. 

However, the custom of certain <term>apothecaries</term> <note>original: "aromatarorium." Literally "dealers in aromatics," referring to those who prepared and sold spices and medicines.</note> is to be condemned, for when they intend to color their balms, they sometimes mix in the most foreign substances; for example, for a Cinnamon Balm, they add the color which they call **Florentine Lake** <note>original: "Lac Florentinum." A red pigment made from organic dyes (like cochineal or kermes) precipitated onto an inorganic base.</note>; for a balm intended to be green, they use some preparation made from **verdigris** <note>original: "viridi æris." Literally "green of copper," a toxic green pigment formed by the action of acetic acid on copper plates.</note>, which everyone knows is corrosive and caustic. True craftsmen...

## CHAPTER FOUR.

### *On the True Essences of Simples and Philosophical Salts.*

**T**ake a herb or whatever <term>simple</term> you wish; crush it, and <term>distill</term> <note>original: "destilla." The process of heating a substance to create vapor and then condensing that vapor into liquid to purify it.</note> water from it. Into this water, place new herbs (though of the same species) that have been crushed. Do this in a well-sealed glass vessel, or in a pot that has another placed over it to serve as a lid. Place it in <term>horse dung</term> <note>original: "fimo equino." Take it out and squeeze out all the juice well through a doubled linen cloth. This pressed juice should be put into a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original: "cucurbitæ." A gourd-shaped chemical vessel used for boiling or distilling.</note> with an <term>alembic</term> <note>original: "alembico." The cap or "head" of a still that collects vapors and directs them into a cooling tube.</note> that has a pointed bottom, as described above, for three days. Let it be cooked gently in a <term>sand bath</term> <note>original: "arena." A container of sand heated from below to provide even, indirect heat to a glass vessel.</note>, so that there is an <term>ascent and descent</term> <note>original: "ascensus & descensus." A process of refluxing, where vapors rise, condense, and drip back down into the liquid to further refine the substance.</note> of the matter, as mentioned before. 

Now, having removed the previous alembic, let a <term>beaked alembic</term> <note>original: "rostratus." An alembic with a long spout or "beak" to direct the distillate away from the heat.</note> be attached along with a <term>receiver</term> <note>original: "recipiente." The vessel placed at the end of the still to collect the condensed liquid.</note>. With all parts properly sealed, let the water be distilled until the matter remaining at the bottom reaches a thick and drier consistency. Let the distilled water be kept for use in a well-sealed glass. Let the matter in the cucurbit be cooled; and when it has been cooled, let it be placed into another cucurbit...

### BOOK V.

***Concerning various rarer and more secret medicines for all diseases of the whole human body, from head to toe.***

P<note>Decorative woodcut initial</note>rior to our undertaking this duty, we wish to warn the Reader that we do not intend here to favor <term>empirics</term> <note>original: "empiricis"; practitioners who relied on experience alone without formal theoretical training, often dismissed as "quacks" by university-educated doctors</note>, who wish to heal the eyes of everyone with a single <term>collyrium</term> <note>original: "collyrio"; a medicinal eye salve or wash</note>, while ignoring the indications and counter-indications of the case. For this reason, we intend that the highly select medicines we provide here be administered only by a Physician, who is capable of knowing the nature and causes of the disease, the affected part, and the <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "temperiem"; the specific balance of "humors" or qualities in an individual patient</note> of the sick person, and so forth. However, as much as can be obtained, we shall not neglect the better specifics and remedies appropriate for any disease, since these are often sought after with great care while others are abandoned. For it must not be thought that everything is to be referred only to those manifest qualities, as some who are proud of their title of wisdom strive to summarize everything into the <term>four humors</term> <note>The traditional medical theory that health is governed by four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, the four qualities <note>Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note>, and as many elements; but they do so in vain.
