# CHAPTER IV.

...and they consist of a watery part, an earthy part, and an intermediate part, which—as Ripley <note>George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist</note> testifies in his *Pupil of Alchemy*—cannot be separated from its extremes, the watery and the earthy, except by the mediation of mercury <note>the alchemical principle of fluidity and transformation</note>. Mercury, as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary 8th-century father of chemistry</note> agrees, retains what is of its own nature, while rejecting what is foreign and exposing it to the fire. This transparent intermediate substance is raised through sublimation <note>the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then becomes solid again upon cooling</note> into a snowy whiteness, secretly containing within itself a sulfurous seed like a tiny, deep red worm: hence it is said in the *Turba* <note>the *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>:
> The Philosophers wondered that redness should exist in such whiteness. <note>original: "Mirati sunt Philosophi, rubedinem in tantâ albedine existere."</note>
Regarding this sulfur, Geber speaks thus in the twenty-eighth chapter of the *Summa* <note>referring to the *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii*, a highly influential medieval work on metallurgy and alchemy</note>:
> By the Most High God, this very thing illuminates and rectifies every body: for it is an alum and a tincture <note>original: "alumen & tinctura"; terms for substances that can fix or change the properties and colors of metals</note>.
This is that water of life, the dry water that does not wet the hands, the congealed water, the animate salt, of which Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century polymath whose name was often used by later alchemists</note> says, following Alphidius <note>an early Arabic alchemical authority</note>:
> Salt is nothing but fire, nor fire anything but sulfur, nor sulfur anything but quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, reduced into that precious, heavenly, and incorruptible substance which we call **our Stone** <note>the "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the Great Work</note>.
For this reason, a certain man alluded to the letters of *Vitriol* in this way: *By **V**isiting the **I**nterior of the **T**erra <note>Earth</note> and by **R**ectifying <note>purifying</note> it, **I**nvenies <note>you will find</note> the **O**ccultum <note>hidden</note> **L**apidem <note>Stone</note>, the **V**eram **M**edicinam <note>True Medicine</note>.* <note>This is a famous alchemical acrostic: V.I.T.R.I.O.L.V.M.</note>

Furthermore, there is a great controversy among practitioners: as to which, among such various kinds of *Vitriol*, is the first...

<insert>
* Which Vitriol is best. <note>original: "Quod Vitriolum optimum"</note>

The Cyprian and Roman varieties ought to be rightly held in suspicion, because they are almost always adulterated, sophisticated, and varied—possessing, namely, different colors, forms, and medicinal powers. Regarding the Hungarian variety, both French and German merchants lie impudently when they sell us a certain blue, transparent Vitriol, sometimes leaning toward green, as the genuine article brought from Pannonia <note>the historical region encompassing modern-day Hungary and parts of its neighbors</note> itself. # CHAPTER IV.

...the first <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of types of vitriol.</note>, which is drawn from Venus <term>Venus</term> <note>The alchemical name for copper.</note>, by the benefit of water, as will be said later. In quality, that which is blue succeeds this one; it contains more of the Sun <term>Sol</term> <note>The alchemical name for gold.</note> within itself; it transmutes more of Mars <term>Mars</term> <note>The alchemical name for iron.</note> into Venus; and it sustains the trials of fire more richly before it gives up its final spirits, from wherever it may be brought.

Therefore, take twelve pounds of this Vitriol and calcine <note>To roast or heat a substance to a high temperature to drive off volatile matter or moisture.</note> it in an earthen vessel over a moderate fire, until all moisture departs. Once the vessel has cooled, reduce the mass—which will be about seven pounds—into a fine powder, along with about one pound of particles from the same vessel; and place it into a strong, luted <note>Sealed with "lute," a clay or paste used to make joints airtight.</note> retort: in such a way, however, that at least a third part remains empty. Place it in a reverberatory furnace <note>A furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat onto the material being processed.</note>, using a large receiver <note>A glass vessel used to collect the distilled product.</note> with a short neck luted on top; and with the joints of the retort and the receiver diligently secured with salt lute, then construct over the retort a wide earthen dish <term>paropsis</term> <note>original: "paropsidem"; a shallow tray or dish used in the laboratory setup.</note>, one foot high, and perforated squarely at the bottom, so that it closes the mouth of the furnace evenly; and at the edges of the furnace, of whatever shape it may be (square or round): fit bricks equal in height to the dish: and fill the space that intervenes between the bricks and the dish with ashes all the way to the top. Then make a chimney from four pieces of brick over the square hole of the vessel, so that the flame, by means of such a vehicle, may be able to escape more freely when the time comes.

# CHAPTER IV.

## Spirit of Niter.

Let Niter <term>Nitrum</term> <note>Also known as saltpeter; chemically, potassium nitrate.</note>, or Saltpeter, be mixed with three parts of common bolus <term>bolus</term> <note>A type of fine, earthy clay used here to prevent the salt from melting into a solid mass during heating.</note>: and let it be distilled through a retort <term>retort</term> <note>A glass or ceramic flask with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</note> for a space of ten or twelve hours. From one pound of Saltpeter, you will receive one pound of spirit, if you have worked well.

This spirit is the true balsamic fire of nature: and it is beneficial for colic, pleurisy, and quinsy <note>original: "anginâ". In this period, this referred to severe throat inflammation or tonsillitis.</note>.

## *Ardent Spirit from Saturn.*

The Calx <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery metallic oxide remains left after a substance has been roasted or burned.</note> of Saturn <term>Saturn</term> <note>The alchemical name for the metal lead.</note>, or minium <term>minium</term> <note>Red lead; lead tetroxide.</note>, is drenched with distilled vinegar or at least its phlegm <term>phlegm</term> <note>The watery, less potent part of a distillate.</note>: afterward, it is digested <term>digeritur</term> <note>Heated gently and steadily to extract soluble materials.</note> for a natural day <note>A 24-hour period.</note> by frequent shaking, so that it does not clump at the bottom of the vessel. The solvent <note>original: "menstruum"</note> is drawn off, and another is substituted until all the saltiness is extracted. 

The depleted liquids are filtered and evaporated by about two-thirds: the crystals are waited for in a cold place and then separated. They are dissolved in new vinegar, filtered, and coagulated as many times as above, until they are sufficiently impregnated with the Salt Ammoniac of vinegar <note>This refers to lead acetate (sugar of lead), which was often described as a salt formed by the union of the metal and the "acid" of vinegar.</note> as if by its own ferment. 

By such heat of a water bath <term>balnei</term> <note>A water bath or bain-marie, providing steady, gentle heat.</note>, they are digested for a month, so that they are perpetually resolved into a liquid like oil. Afterward, let them be distilled through a retort in a sand bath <note>original: "in arenâ"</note>, observing the degrees of fire and using a wide receiver <note>The vessel that collects the distillate.</note>; for unless it is very diligently sealed <note>original: "lutetur"</note> to the retort with lute <note>A chemical paste or cement used to seal joints.</note>, such a great fragrance fills the whole laboratory and is lost, that I do not doubt but that it...

## CHAPTER V.
->*Concerning Vinegar.*<-

### *Distilled Vinegar.*

**V**inegar is distilled without digestion <term>digestion</term> <note>The process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat to soften it or encourage chemical change.</note> in the same way as wine; except that the phlegm <term>phlegm</term> <note>The watery, tasteless, and medically inactive part of a distillate.</note> comes out first, as it does in all other acidic things, whereas the spirit <term>spirit</term> <note>The active, volatile essence of the substance.</note> comes out last. Oil and Salt are extracted in the same manner as was described concerning wine.

### *Alkalized Vinegar.*

Once vinegar has been distilled to the consistency of liquid honey, common water is poured over it so that it stands at a palm’s height above the substance. It is then digested in a bath <term>balneo</term> <note>A water bath or "bain-marie," used to provide gentle, even heat.</note> for two days. It is then placed in a cold spot so that it may produce crystals; the water is poured off by tilting the vessel <note>Decanting.</note>, and fresh water is poured on until all oiliness has departed. Then the crystals are repeatedly dissolved in boiling water and coagulated in the cold, so that they are rendered entirely transparent. Then vinegar, which has been distilled four times and cleared of all phlegm, is poured over them, in such a proportion that four parts of vinegar are added to one pound of crystals. These are distilled in a retort <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances.</note> through a sand bath <note>A container of sand heated by a furnace, providing a more intense and even heat than water.</note>, giving a strong enough fire toward the end of the process. When this is done, the dregs are calcined <term>calcined</term> <note>Heated to a high temperature in the air to reduce the substance to ashes or powder.</note>, the fixed salt is extracted, and the vinegar, animated by the essential salt, is rectified <term>rectified</term> <note>Purified by repeated distillation.</note>;

### CHAPTER VI.

#### Concerning Oils.

**O**il is most properly defined as that which is pressed from olives, being devoid of any extreme quality; regarding all other substances, however, the term is used only by analogy. All oils exist somewhere between the natures of air and fire: the sharper they are, the more fiery they are judged to be; the less sharp they are, the more ethereal and airy they are considered.

### *Oil of Turpentine*

Take the residue <note>original: "medullam," literally marrow or core</note> remaining from the distillation of spirit of Turpentine; distill it through ashes <note>using a sand or ash bath to provide indirect, even heat</note> in a retort by itself. In this way, when the oil has been extracted, Colophony <term>colophony</term> <note>Also known as rosin; the solid resin remaining after the distillation of turpentine.</note> will remain at the bottom of the retort. It warms, softens, disperses, opens, and cleanses; and externally it can be used in place of a true balsam in all wounds, malignant <term>cacoethes</term> <note>A medical term for a stubborn, bad-natured, or pre-cancerous ulcer.</note>, incurable, and foul-smelling ulcers—such as fistulas, lupus <note>here referring to "the wolf," a historical term for corrosive skin ulcers</note>, and similar spreading sores <term>phagedenic</term> <note>From the Greek for "to eat"; ulcers that rapidly destroy surrounding tissue.</note>—as well as for swellings behind the ears, fractures, muscle contractions, etc. However, it does not always perform these things when used alone; rather, it is further required that it be suitably mixed with other ingredients fit for curing the condition.

### *Oil of Cloves*

Take four pounds of coarsely crushed cloves <note>original: "Caryophyllorum"</note> and forty pounds of spring water. Macerate <note>soak to soften</note> them in a warm place for a sufficient time; add two ounces of Tartar <note>potassium bitartrate, often used as a catalyst or to adjust the acidity in distillations</note>; afterward, distill them through a copper still <note>original: "vesicam aeneam"</note> equipped with a cooling apparatus, and you will have eight ounces of oil. In the same manner, mace, pepper, anise seed, coriander, etc., are distilled.

It is beneficial for cold diseases of the stomach, the liver, the heart, and for diarrhea caused by cold humors; it dissipates melancholic spirits and clarifies those that are thick <note>In the humoral system, "thick" or "gross" spirits were thought to cause mental sluggishness or depression</note>.

### *Oil of Sugar*

Take 4 ounces of white sugar <term>Sacchari albi</term> <note>Pure cane sugar was a luxury item often used as a base for medicines.</note> coarsely pounded.
->*8 ounces of Aqua Vitae.*<-
<note>original: "Aquæ vitæ"; literally "water of life," referring to concentrated distilled alcohol or brandy.</note>

It strengthens; and by a proven experiment <note>original: "certo experimento"</note>, it aids those suffering from a cough due to a chill of the lungs.

### *Oil of Tartar*

This oil—in addition to the method mentioned above regarding its spirit—is also made by deliquescence <term>per deliquium</term> <note>A process where a solid substance absorbs enough atmospheric moisture to dissolve completely into a liquid.</note>, by placing tartar <term>Tartarum</term> <note>The hard crust (potassium bitartrate) found in wine barrels; once burned or "calcined," it becomes potassium carbonate, which absorbs water easily.</note> calcined to whiteness in a cellar or another damp place until it resolves into an oil, which must then be filtered. It can also be prepared if the tartar, after calcination, is dissolved in common water, filtered, and coagulated <note>thickened or dried</note>, and then placed in a damp spot until it resolves.
It is an excellent remedy for all spreading sores <term>serpiginibus</term> <note>From the Latin "serpere," to creep; refers to skin conditions like ringworm or herpes that spread across the skin.</note>, ulcers (especially venereal ones), ringworm <term>tinea</term>, scabies, and warts. It smooths wrinkles from the face <note>original: "Faciem erugat"</note> and makes the skin soft.

### *Oil of Amber*

Digest 1 pound of crushed amber <term>Succini</term> <note>Fossilized resin; in alchemy, it was prized for its "volatile salt" and oil.</note> in 1 pound of white wine. Then add a handful of prepared salt; distill through a retort <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</note>, observing the various degrees of heat <note>Starting with low heat and gradually increasing it.</note>. It is rectified <note>purified</note> by distilling it twice more with salt only.

Heat pieces of bricks, or flints the size of beans, in a crucible until they are white-hot. Cast them while thus ignited into old olive oil; cover it and leave it overnight. ## *Oil of Salt.*

Salt consists of different parts: earthy, watery, and fiery. Its consistency and solidity come from the earth, its solubility from water, and its sharp bite from fire. It is acrid, **bittersweet** <note>original: "γλυκύπικρος" (glykypikros)</note>, sharp, subtle, penetrating, pure, fragrant, incombustible, and preserves other things from corruption. It is transparent like the air. Through repeated preparations, it becomes dissolvable in moisture and liquefiable in fire like metals. It is, as it were, like a soul in a body, according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author who wrote the "Natural History."</note>, who (following the Stoic philosophers) says: salt was given to the flesh of a pig <note>Pliny famously wrote that salt acts like a soul for a pig's body, keeping the meat from rotting while the animal is still alive.</note>...

# CHAPTER VII.
## On Liquid Tinctures.

**B**y the word Tincture <term>Tinctura</term>, Chemists do not mean—as the common people suppose—simple colors separated from a mixture or merely brightened. Rather, they mean the colors of the essences of things and their formal qualities, which have been extracted from a solid body <note>original: "è concreto corpore"; refers to the physical or "concrete" material of the plant or mineral.</note>. For this reason, Tinctures are sometimes called oils, sometimes Spirits, and sometimes the fifth essence <term>quinta essentia</term> <note>The "quintessence" or most purified, spiritualized part of a substance, beyond the four physical elements.</note>.

### *Tincture of Dried Roses.*

Place one ounce of dried red roses into four pounds of warm water, to which you should add about two drachms <note>A drachm is a small unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce or 3.9 grams.</note> of spirit of Vitriol or Sulfur <note>These are acidic solutions—essentially sulfuric acid—used here to help extract the deep red color from the rose petals.</note>. Within three or four hours, the water will become very deeply colored and should then be filtered. If you dissolve twelve ounces of sugar into this, you will have a true cooling remedy for the liver <note>In the medical theories of the time, the liver was often seen as a source of excess "heat" in the body; "refrigerative" medicines were used to balance this.</note>.

### *Tincture of Violets.*

Let crushed flowers be macerated <note>Soaked to soften and extract the active ingredients.</note> in their own distilled water, or in the "oil of sugar" described above; afterward, let them be squeezed out. Let the liquid expressed from them be strained until the tincture meets your requirements.

-> OR: <-

Place the flowers at the beak of the alembic <term>alembici rostris</term> <note>An alembic is a distilling apparatus; the "beak" is the tube through which the vapor travels. This method uses the rising steam to pull the essence from the flowers.</note> so that the distilled water, as it passes by, carries the tincture away with it.

# CHAPTER VIII.
## On Balsams.

**C**hemical Balsams <term>Balsami Chymici</term> are nothing other than compound oils that have been made thicker by the addition of other substances. They generally consist of three types of liquid: a spirituous or watery part, an oily part, and a thick part like <note>original: "instar"</note> honey. To these, depending on the nature of the thing, musk, ambergris, civet, and similar substances are sometimes added <note>Musk, ambergris, and civet are aromatic substances derived from animals, highly prized in early modern medicine and perfumery for their potency.</note>.

### *Cinnamon Balsam.*

This is composed of a tincture—extracted by spirit of wine <note>Distilled alcohol, used as a powerful solvent.</note> and then thickened—along with the oil and the salt of the same cinnamon <note>The "salt" refers to the mineral components extracted from the plant's ashes after burning, which alchemists believed held the physical "body" or stability of the medicine.</note>, as well as white wax. The wax should be thoroughly dissolved and washed in rose water and cleared of all sharpness <note>The "sharpness" or acidity of the wax was removed to prevent skin irritation.</note>, which gives the mixture a medium consistency. Alternatively, it can be made from the suet of a deer or a sheep, carefully cleaned and washed. In this way, any of these ingredients can be mixed on their own, or together with the wax, and afterwards reduced to the proper consistency with the extract, oil, and salt. In the same manner, Balsams are prepared from Cloves <term>Garyophyllis</term>, juniper, sage, rosemary, anise, and similar plants, which are most effective both for external application and internal use.

### *Balsam of Sulfur.*

Take two ounces of flowers of sulfur <term>florum Sulphuris</term> <note>Not a plant, but a bright yellow powder formed by heating sulfur until it turns to vapor and then solidifies.</note> and four ounces of Oil of Turpentine.
Mix them: and place the glass vessel in a sand bath <note>A "sand bath" or "arena" involved placing the vessel in a container of sand heated by a fire, ensuring even, gentle heat without breaking the glass.</note>, so that it may bubble slowly for the space of eight hours, and become...

## *Balsam of Saturn* <note>In alchemy, "Saturn" is the symbolic name for the metal Lead.</note>

Distill two parts of vinegar impregnated with the salt of Saturn <term>sale Saturni</term> <note>Lead acetate, also known as "sugar of lead." Though lead is toxic, it was commonly used in early medicine for its cooling and anti-inflammatory properties when applied externally.</note> so that only a third part remains. Then take four ounces of rose oil and eight ounces of the impregnated vinegar. Pour this drop by drop over the oil: and at the same time mix it continuously in a bronze mortar <note>A bowl for grinding and mixing ingredients with a pestle.</note> until it becomes like an ointment. This is beneficial for inflammations and "hot" gout <term>podagræ calidæ</term> <note>Gout was often categorized as "hot" or "cold" based on the Four Humors theory; hot gout involved redness and swelling.</note>. If the same vinegar impregnated with the salt of Saturn is mixed with an equal part of common water and applied warm with folded linen cloths upon bruises on any part of the body, it immediately soothes all pain.

# CHAPTER IX.

## On Extracts.

**E**XTRACTS specifically so-called are prepared from the animal and vegetable kingdoms, by the benefit of suitable solvents or menstruums <term>menstruorum</term> <note>In early chemistry, a "menstruum" is a solvent used to extract the active "virtues" or essences from a solid substance.</note>, such as spirit of juniper wine <note>original: "spiritus vini juniperi"</note>, whey <note>original: "serum lactis"</note>, vinous mead <note>original: "hydromel vinosum"</note>, water of fragrant apples, fumitory <note>original: "fumi terrae," a plant used in traditional medicine for its cleansing properties.</note> and the like, or distilled water made from the same things one intends to extract. From animals, the flesh—or mummy <note>original: "Mumia." In this period, "mummy" referred to a medicine made from embalmed human remains or bitumen, thought to have profound healing powers.</note>, liver, spleen, lungs, testicles, and similar parts—are selected. From these, certain preparations have become widely famous: extracts from the human skull for epilepsy; from the spleen of an ox to promote menstruation; from the liver of a calf for dropsy <note>original: "hydropem," an old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note> and hepatic flux <note>A condition involving chronic discharge or dysfunction of the liver.</note>; and from the lung of a fox for asthma and similar diseases. From the vegetable kingdom, various extracts are made: namely from herbs, flowers, roots, juices, berries, barks, woods, spices, seeds, and fruits. These can be seen in the works of Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a physician who advocated for the use of chemical remedies alongside traditional herbal ones.</note> in the final chapter of his *Restored Pharmacopoeia of the Dogmatics*.

Furthermore, for preparing purging <note>Laxative.</note> extracts, many have hitherto used spirit of wine <note>Distilled alcohol.</note> as the solvent. However, because this greatly weakens their cathartic <term>catharticam</term> power; promi- <note>The text cuts off here; the full word is likely "promiscue," meaning indiscriminately or generally.</note>

indiscriminately <note>The Latin text begins with the end of the word "promiscuè" from the previous page.</note> in all things, it does not seem it should be used. It may be employed at times in the extract of Hellebore, Colocynth <note>A bitter plant used as a powerful purgative.</note>, or Scammony <note>A resinous root used in traditional medicine as a laxative.</note>; but in others, distilled waters should be substituted. For instance, for Rhubarb, endive water will be suitable; for Eastern Senna leaves, the water of fragrant apples, fumitory, or fennel; for Agaric <note>A type of fungus found on larch trees, historically used as a medicinal purge.</note>, cinnamon water; and so on, matching others to others.

Now, if such a "water of life" <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>At this time, "aqua vitae" usually referred to concentrated alcohol or brandy.</note>—specifically one deprived of its sal ammoniac <note>original: "sale armoniaco," ammonium chloride, used in various chemical processes.</note>, as Dariotus, and after him Johannes du Val (a physician of Issoudun), and also Penotus in his treatise on the true preparation of chemical medicines, teach regarding the Mastery of Tartar <term>magisterio Tartari</term>—could be provided, nothing better could be desired for preparing extracts of every kind.

However, although Mr. Mayaud—a man long experienced in chemical matters and a singular friend of mine—tried with me to prepare such a solvent according to the pleasure of those learned men, we nevertheless "lost both our oil and our labor" <note>original: "oleum & operam perdidimus," a Latin idiom meaning to waste time, effort, and resources on a fruitless task.</note> in this operation. From this, one might conjecture that while the good Penotus, in the aforementioned Mastery of Tartar, warns and invites others to the fear of God and to give thanks for such a rare secret, he himself perhaps did not fear God enough, nor did he give Him thanks, when he consecrated such a "mastery" to posterity <note>The author is politely accusing Penotus of publishing a recipe that does not actually work.</note>.

## Extract of Rhubarb.

Digest fresh Rhubarb, cut into tiny pieces, in endive water or another fragrant water until it becomes colored. Pour off the colored liquid and pour on new water as many times as necessary until the water no longer takes on any color. Filter the pourings, circulate them, and draw off the solvent <term>menstruum</term> <note>In early chemistry, a "menstruum" is any liquid used to dissolve a solid or extract its "virtues."</note> using a water bath until it reaches the consistency of an extract. Be sure to add the salt from the dregs beforehand, as described in the preparation above.

# CHAPTER X.

## *On soft Tinctures,*

**A**LTHOUGH TINCTURES might rightly be categorized as <term>extracts</term> <note>concentrated substances obtained by using a solvent</note> because of the operations by which they are perfected and their consistency; nevertheless, because they have been granted the title of "tinctures" by authors, it was decided to assign them their own special chapter.

## *Tincture of honey.*

Mix honey with well-cleaned sand <note>Adding sand to sticky honey increases the surface area, allowing the alcohol to filter through and extract the nutrients more effectively.</note> until it becomes a sort of mass. Pour <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>distilled alcohol</note> over it so that it rises two fingers [above the mass]. <term>Digest</term> <note>steep in gentle heat</note> for five or six hours. Pour off the colored spirit and pour on more, until it is no longer colored. Filter the tinted spirit and thicken it. It nourishes those suffering from <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "phthisicos." A historical term for wasting diseases, usually pulmonary tuberculosis.</note> in a wonderful way.

## *Tincture of Saffron.*

It is made with spirit of wine, which must be poured over it as many times as necessary until it has drawn out the entire tincture and the <term>earth</term> <note>the solid plant residue left after extraction</note> remains whitish. The tincture is filtered, and the <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original abbreviation: "S. V." for spiritus vini</note> is drawn off with the light heat of a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "balnei."</note>. It possesses various and excellent powers; it wonderfully refreshes and restores the spirits, especially in those prone to <term>fainting</term> <note>original: "syncopticis." Refers to syncope or fainting spells.</note>, if even a single drop of it is administered in broth or white wine.

## Tincture of Sugar.

Take one pound of powdered white sugar: put it in a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</note>, or a <term>matrass</term> <note>a long-necked glass flask</note> with two spoonfuls of distilled vinegar: <term>digest</term> <note>to steep a substance in a solvent using gentle heat to extract its properties</note> over hot ashes for six hours: then pour over rectified <term>aqua vitae</term> <note>literally "water of life"; a term for highly concentrated distilled alcohol</note>, so that it floats two fingers above [the sugar], digest until it is colored: afterward pour off the tinted water, and pour on more as many times as needed until it is no longer colored. Then draw off the <term>menstruum</term> <note>the solvent used for extraction</note> through a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "balneum." A method of heating a vessel by placing it in hot water to ensure even, gentle temperature.</note>. A red tincture or essence will remain at the bottom, which should be <term>circulated</term> <note>a process where vapors are condensed and returned to the same vessel to refine the mixture</note> with cordial waters.

It is beneficial in <term>syncope</term> <note>fainting</note> and swooning, administered with cinnamon and rose water.

## Tincture of Sulfur.

Melt <term>salt of Tartar</term> <note>potassium carbonate, often used as a purifying agent</note> in a <term>crucible</term> <note>original: "tigillo." A container used for melting substances at very high heat.</note>: likewise <term>flowers of sulfur</term> <note>a fine yellow powder produced by the sublimation of sulfur</note> in another crucible: afterward mix them together and allow to cool naturally. Grind the mass, over which pour <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>distilled ethanol</note> to a height of four fingers. Digest until it is tinted a very deep red color: draw off the separated solvent through a water bath. This tincture is a true <term>balsam</term> for the lungs.

## Tincture of Coral.

Dissolve two ounces of coral in one pound of lemon juice, digesting for eight days, and afterward filtering. In this tincture dissolve eight ounces of white sugar, and digest by evaporating to the consistency of a syrup.

Dose: one spoonful in every <term>hepatic flux</term> <note>original: "fluxu hepatico." A historical term for a persistent discharge or chronic diarrhea believed to be caused by liver malfunction.</note>

# CHAPTER XI.

**O**N the <term>Calcination</term> <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in a crucible to remove volatile components or change its chemical state</note> of Common Salt, Saltpeter, Vitriol, Sponge Stone, Crystal, and Silver Marcasite.

## *The Calcination of Common Salt.*

Common salt is placed in a <term>crucible</term> <note>a heat-resistant ceramic container</note>, or another earthenware vessel, filled almost to the top and covered; it is set among burning coals until it glows red-hot all over and no longer crackles <note>this crackling is known as "decrepitation," caused by water trapped inside the salt crystals expanding and bursting</note>. Afterward, it is dissolved in common water; filtered; and <term>coagulated</term> <note>thickened or crystallized by evaporating the liquid</note> in a new glazed dish.

## *The Calcination of Saltpeter: otherwise called Mineral Crystal, or Lapis Prunella.*

This salt, in the weight of half a <term>drachm</term> <note>an apothecary measurement roughly equal to 1/8th of an ounce</note>, dissolved in rose or endive water, is the greatest secret for <term>prunella</term> <note>a historical term for a painful, burning sore throat or "thrush" in the mouth</note>. Taken with <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>highly concentrated alcohol</note>, it settles a cough. When taken with hyssop water, it clears obstructions of both the lungs and the liver; it cures difficulty in breathing; and it restores a lost voice, making it resonant—provided that half a drachm of it is taken daily in the morning on an empty stomach with a moderately boiled egg yolk <note>original: "ovi vitello"</note>. It is also effective in many other diseases, both internal and external, as Johannes Tholdeus <note>Johann Thölde, a salt-maker and chemist often credited with publishing the "Basil Valentine" texts</note> teaches at greater length in his *Halographia* <note>original: "Halographia," a treatise on salts</note>, and as Bernhardus Penotus <note>Bernard Georges Penot, a 16th-century French physician and alchemist</note> teaches in his work on the preparation of chemical medicines.

### *Calcination of Sponge-Stone.*

The <term>Sponge-Stone</term> <note>stony concretions sometimes found within sea sponges, or fossilized echinoids, traditionally used to treat urinary complaints</note> is heated in the fire: and is quenched in distilled vinegar as many times as necessary: until it is reduced to a <term>calx</term> <note>a fine powder or "lime" produced by intense heating</note>. Its use in calcination is for extracting a <term>tincture</term> <note>a medicinal extract dissolved in alcohol or another solvent</note>.

### *Calcination of Crystal.*

Crystal <note>usually clear quartz</note>, having been <term>reverberated</term> <note>heated in a furnace where the flames are "reverberated" or deflected off the roof onto the substance</note> in a crucible for six hours, should be reduced to a fine powder; and mix this with an equal amount <note>original: "ana"</note> of <term>saltpeter</term> <note>potassium nitrate</note>: and reverberate it again with a powerful fire for eighteen hours. Cast the melted substance into <term>heavenly water</term> <note>original: "aquam cælestem"; likely referring to distilled rainwater, considered by alchemists to have special properties</note>: and whatever remains undissolved, dry it and reduce it to an <term>Alcohol</term> <note>in this period, "alcohol" referred to any substance—solid or liquid—refined to its most subtle, impalpable powder form</note>. Then boil it with the same water: until it thickens like a paste; and spread it over pieces of glass, in a warm place, so that it may dry: and again reduce it to a fine powder: and if you wish, place it in a damp place, so that it may dissolve <note>by absorbing moisture from the air, a process called deliquescence</note>. If any part remains undissolved: by repeating the calcination with <term>nitre</term> <note>another name for saltpeter</note> and the other steps, as described above, it will become soluble.

The dose is three or four drops, with an equal amount of oil of juniper, against stones of the kidneys and bladder.

### *Another Way.*

Heat a clear and heavy Crystal until it glows white: and quench it in distilled vinegar as many times as necessary: until it is reduced to a powder with the slightest touch. Then mix it with an equal amount of Saltpeter, and reverberate it for eighteen hours.

# CHAPTER XII.

## On the Calcination of Antimony.

### *The Calcination of Antimony.*

**T**ake four pounds of choice <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "Stibium"; a brittle, silvery-gray metalloid used in medicines, though toxic if improperly prepared</note> and five pounds of prepared salt. Once they are powdered, let them be mixed: and in a wide, flat-bottomed earthen vessel, let them be agitated over a <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>a furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat from the roof onto the material being heated</note>, moving them continuously with an iron spatula for the space of five or six hours, until the smoke ceases and the antimony becomes white and yellowish. (Care must be taken diligently to avoid melting the material and to avoid the noxious smoke). 

Afterward, let them be ground into a powder, and let the salt be drawn out by the pouring on of hot water and, more frequently, cold water. Once this is dried and powdered, <term>sublime</term> <note>to heat a solid until it turns into a gas and then hardens back into a solid on a cooler surface, purifying it</note> it for ten or twelve hours. Having collected the <term>flowers</term> <note>the fine, purified powder that settles at the top of a vessel after sublimation</note>, grind the <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>literally "dead head"; the useless residue remaining at the bottom of the vessel after the active parts have been extracted</note>: and for the space of a month, heat it to redness in a <term>reverberatory</term> vessel, which must be closed up to keep out ashes so that the fire is not hindered from its proper operation. 

After this <term>calcination</term> <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its physical or chemical state</note>, extract the tincture with <term>radical vinegar</term> <note>original: "aceto radicato"; a very strong, concentrated vinegar used as a powerful solvent</note>: and further process it by filtration, separation of the <term>menstruum</term> <note>a solvent used to extract or dissolve materials</note>, and <term>circulation</term> <note>a process of continuous distillation where the vapor returns to the liquid in a closed loop</note> with <term>cordial water</term> <note>a medicinal liquid intended to invigorate the heart or spirit</note>.

The dose for more robust people is four or five grains; for the weaker, two or three grains, administered in a cooked apple or in a <term>conserve of roses</term> <note>a medicinal jam made of rose petals and sugar</note>.

## *Star-like Regulus of Mars.*
<note>In alchemy, "Mars" is the name for iron. A "Regulus" or "Little King" is the metallic mass that settles at the bottom of the crucible during smelting. The "star-like" quality refers to a crystalline pattern that forms on the surface of the metal when it is purified to a high degree.</note>

Repeat this four, five, or six times, until you have the star-like Regulus of Mars.

## CHAPTER XIII.

### On the Calcination and Preparation of Mercury.

**M**ercury <margin>natural mercury</margin> is a mineral body, composed of a subtle sulfurous earth and a strongly admixed water. Its earthy substance, however, must be purged of its thick, sulfurous earthiness; and its watery substance must be freed from superfluous humidity. It is of two kinds: <margin>the substance of mercury</margin> natural and artificial. Natural mercury, which is active and highly purified, is found in Almagro <note>a town in the province of Ciudad Real, Spain, famous for its mercury mines</note> near Calatrava, in the kingdom of Castile. It is found "living" <note>original: "vivus"; referring to liquid elemental mercury, often called quicksilver</note>, flowing by itself, or coagulated in Cinnabar <note>the bright red ore (mercury sulfide) from which mercury is extracted</note>, from which it is drawn out by the force of fire. This most ancient mineral was called by Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note> the "vomit of eternal liquid" <note>original: "vomicam liquoris æterni"</note>. A similar kind is found in Idria, a village in the county of Goritz in Slavonia <note>modern-day Slovenia; the Idrija mine was the second largest mercury mine in the world</note>. But the Spanish variety excels in quality, although Idria is far more fertile. 

It is, however, a thing worthy of admiration that although a pestilential plague <note>original: "lues pestifera"</note> rages almost every single year in the vicinity of Idria, that place itself remains immune to it. This was solemnly confirmed to me eight years ago when I traveled there, both by men of advanced age who had observed it themselves and by what they had learned from their ancestors. From this it is sufficiently clear—as well as from countless other examples—that Mercury is the supreme [enemy] of all corruption <note>The text cuts off here at the word "corruptionis"; the author is arguing that mercury's purity and volatile nature allow it to resist or prevent decay and disease</note>...

## CHAPTER XIII.

Another Mercury is found on the mountain called Gimnauvoda <note>likely Zimna Woda, meaning "Cold Water" in Polish</note>, six miles from Kraków, in Poland, located between Tarnawa, Rybie, and Strzelecki, which spontaneously erupts to the surface of the earth at certain times of the year: especially in the autumn; although around the feast of St. John the Baptist <note>Midsummer, June 24th</note>, I have also collected many grains, like peas, among the roots of the grasses there. But this Mercury is too watery, and far inferior to the Slavonian as well as the Spanish. It is also found naturally in many other places: and sometimes in gold and silver mines.

<margin>a</margin> Artificial <margin>a</margin> <note>original: "Mercurius artificialis"</note> mercury is made in a manner common enough and well-known to craftsmen, through reviving salts <note>original: "sales resuscitativos"</note> [extracted] both from mineral intermediates and from metals. Indeed, in this city <note>Paris, where the author Jean Beguin taught</note> I have known several men worthy of trust and of particular authority and standing, who have drawn out "living" mercury <note>liquid quicksilver</note> not only from minerals, but even from previously calcined human blood, and even from plants.

### Recipe for Mercury.

Take one pound of distilled vinegar: put it in a strong <term>matrass</term> <note>original: "matratio"; a long-necked glass flask used for heating liquids</note> with a handful of prepared salt: stir vigorously for a quarter of an hour so that they are mixed and the vinegar is blackened. Pour this off by tilting the vessel with the <term>Mercury</term> into a glazed dish, and wash it with warm water as many times as necessary until all the blackness and saltiness is separated. Once dried, put it back into the <term>matrass</term> with vinegar and salt as described above, repeating the same labor three or four times, and finally passing it through leather <note>squeezing mercury through chamois or soft leather acts as a fine filter to remove solid contaminants</note>.

<margin>a Purification of Mercury.</margin>

But this is a common and imperfect purification: a more perfect one follows: Take <term>precipitated Mercury</term>, <term>cinnabarized</term> <note>mercury recovered from cinnabar (mercury sulfide)</note>, or <term>sublimated</term>: mix it with two parts of its own weight of <term>burnt Tartar</term> <note>potassium carbonate produced by burning the crusty deposits from wine barrels</note> or <term>quicklime</term>: distill through a glass <term>retort</term> <note>a flask with a long, downward-curved neck</note> using a <term>fire of suppression</term> <note>original: "igne suppressionis"; a heating method where the vessel is covered or surrounded by coals to drive vapors downward</note>, or in a <term>closed reverberatory furnace</term> <note>a furnace where the heat is reflected or "reverberated" from the roof onto the vessel</note>, with a large receiver half-full of water attached. In this way, you will receive <term>Mercury</term> more purified than by the previous method. 

But the most perfect way of purifying <term>Mercury</term>, than which no better can be given, is its <term>amalgamation</term> <note>the process of bonding mercury with another metal</note> with perfect bodies <note>in alchemy, "perfect bodies" typically refers to gold and silver</note>: by distilling it several times through a <term>retort</term>, [removing] at each turn the earthy, sulfurous, and foul-smelling dregs...

# CHAPTER XIII.

## *White Precipitate*

<term>Mercury</term> is dissolved in <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aqua forti"; literally "strong water," refers to nitric acid</note>, and by the pouring on of salt water it is precipitated into a white powder. The dissolving liquid is poured off by tilting the vessel: and the precipitate is deprived of all saltiness and sharpness <note>acidity or corrosiveness</note> by many washings combined with <term>digestion</term> <note>the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat</note>. Finally, once dried, it is washed with rose water and dried again. The internal dose is between eight to ten grains, especially in venereal diseases <note>such as syphilis</note>: it purges only through the lower parts <note>the bowels</note>.

## *Red Precipitate.*

After the dissolution of <term>Mercury</term> in <term>aqua fortis</term>, let an evaporation to dryness be performed with a violent fire: in the bottom of the <term>matrass</term> <note>a long-necked glass bulb used for heating</note> will remain a red precipitated powder, most suitable for ulcers, especially those of a venereal nature.

## *Precipitated Mercury.*
### THE BEST OF THE BEST.

Take four <term>ounces</term> <note>original: "uncias"; a unit of weight</note> of purified Mercury: pour on eight ounces of rectified <term>oil of sulfur</term> <note>concentrated sulfuric acid</note>. Digest for two days in a sand bath: then distill through a <term>retort</term>, with three <term>cohobations</term> <note>the process of pouring the distilled liquid back onto the solid residue and re-distilling it to increase potency</note>; lastly, use a violent fire so that the retort glows red-hot. Remove and grind the white mass: wash it repeatedly with warm distilled water until you see the precipitate turned into a very yellow powder: over which you should burn <term>spirits of wine</term> <note>original: "Spiritum vini"; high-proof ethanol</note> three times. In this way, it can be safely given into the body. The dose is from three or four to six grains, administered in extracts.

## Another Method.

Dissolve Mercury <note>quicksilver</note> in <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "aqua forti"; nitric acid</note>, and precipitate it—as is the custom of the art—by evaporating all moisture, so that the precipitate becomes red. Once powdered, place it into a strong <term>matrass</term> <note>a long-necked glass flask</note>, pouring over it <term>vinegar</term> <note>original: "acetnm," likely a typo for "acetum"</note> distilled three times, so that it stands above the powder to the height of five fingers. Apply heat via a sand bath so that the vinegar boils slowly for the space of six hours, and the precipitate is entirely dissolved. Into this solution (having first been filtered), pour a liquid impregnated with the <term>soul of the world</term> <note>original: "animâ mundi"; in alchemy, this refers to a vitalizing universal spirit or a powerful solvent believed to be the essence of nature</note>: and the Mercury will immediately be separated from the solvent; it must then be washed and dried. The dose is from 4 to 5 grains.

Then, having removed it from the fire, grind it into a fine powder and place it in a matrass: pour over it rectified <term>aqua regia</term> <note>original: "aquam Regis"; "royal water," a highly corrosive mixture of acids</note>, digesting it for twenty-four hours. Afterward, pour off the tinted water by <term>inclination</term> <note>carefully tilting the vessel to pour off liquid without disturbing the sediment</note>, and pour on fresh water as many times as necessary until it has extracted all the <term>tincture</term> <note>the infused color or medicinal essence</note>. Distill these extracts until they reach an oily consistency. Take one ounce of this oil and pour it over [four]...

# CHAPTER XIV.

### *On the Calcination of Saturn and Jupiter.*
<note>In alchemy, Saturn refers to Lead and Jupiter refers to Tin. Calcination is the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder or ash.</note>

**S**ince, according to the testimony of Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century scholar often considered the father of chemistry</note>, the dissolving of bodies is impossible if their composition is unknown: before we approach the calcinations of metals, we must speak briefly of their nature.
<margin>a The generation of metals.</margin>
Indeed, Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the "Hermetic" or alchemical tradition</note>, that father of Philosophers, seems to me to have perceived rightly when he says: *That which is above is like that which is below: and vice-versa.* <note>original: "Id quod est superius, est sicut id, quod est inferius"; the famous opening of the Emerald Tablet, suggesting a correspondence between the heavens and the earth.</note> For in the same way that nature, little by little and successively, produces plants and other vegetables on the surface of the earth, so in subterranean places she generates metals—though more slowly and over a longer span of time—from a moist, oily vapor of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note> and <term>vitriolic sulfur</term> <note>a type of sulfur associated with the acidic and transformative power of vitriol</note>, which contains within itself the properties of mercury cooked down <note>original: "decoquentis"; a term for natural heat refining a substance</note> by its own heat. Hence Quicksilver is called the Mother of Metals, while Sulfur is the Father; and in them are the four elements, which [form] the nature of all bodies...

# CHAPTER XIV.

...[mine]ral matters are represented. For Mercury, like a female, cold and moist, represents the nature of water and air; while sulfur, like a male, hot and dry, takes the place of fire and earth. If anyone wishes to establish their matter as not so much a breath <note>original: "halitum"; often used in alchemy to describe vapors or exhalations rising within the earth</note> but rather a juice, I will not object.

For when last summer I descended into a silver mine in Hungary, about half a mile from <term>Schemnitz</term> <note>Modern Banská Štiavnica in Slovakia, a major center for silver and gold mining in the early modern period</note>, roughly one thousand five hundred cubits deep: I learned from the miners—who worked stripped of their clothes and even their shirts due to the extreme heat of the ore—that mineral vapors are frequently carried upward from the center of the earth. These vapors extinguish their lamps and even the men themselves if they do not withdraw quickly. Some time later, however, in that same place, those vapors are found to have congealed on the walls of the mine into a mass which, at a light touch, flows like oil. 

From this, one might perhaps infer that vapor is the **more remote matter** of metals, while the sulfurous and mercurial juice is the **more proximate matter**. And I have at hand, from that same mine and others, flints <note>original: "silices"; here referring to the hard, silica-rich rocks or ores found in the mines</note> which such moist, oily mineral vapor or juice has penetrated everywhere. In some of these, raw matter is seen that is not sufficiently "cooked" <note>original: "cocta"; the alchemical theory of "coction" suggested that metals matured in the earth over long periods of time through natural heat</note>; in others, it is moderately cooked, from one pound of which can be extracted six drachms <note>A drachm is an ancient unit of weight; in this context, roughly 4 grams</note> of pure silver and about half a scruple <note>A scruple is about 1.3 grams</note> of gold; in others, it is perfectly cooked: so...

Even though there are some who, because of certain trifling arguments, deny that Mercury and Sulfur are the basic matter of metals: it is nevertheless better to believe the metallic Philosophers and the metallurgists, who testify with one voice that these are found in all mines and veins. Smelters, roasters, and assayers of metals agree with this opinion; not to mention that Physicians observe that most diseases of miners arise from raw Sulfurous and Mercurial vapors admitted into the body, and that metals, in external applications, perform the same effects as Quicksilver <note>original: "Hydrargyrum"</note>. Indeed, all metals can be reduced into quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> with little effort, and quicksilver back into all metals.

### *The Calcination of Saturn*
<note>In alchemy, "Saturn" is the traditional name for the metal Lead.</note>

Lead is melted in an earthen vessel or an iron pot and is purged of dross <term>scoriae</term> <note>the refuse or slag left over after smelting metal</note>. Then, the fire having been increased until the pot glows white-hot, and with continuous stirring with an iron spatula, it is reduced into a powder <term>calx</term>; which, once sifted through a fine sieve, becomes red lead <term>minium</term> if it is further heated in a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace where the flame is "reverberated" or reflected down onto the material being heated</note> for a longer time.

### *The Calcination of Jupiter*
<note>In alchemy, "Jupiter" is the traditional name for the metal Tin.</note>

Take four pounds of unadulterated English Tin (which you will recognize by its weight and its reaction to being hammered). Melt it in a flat-bottomed pot and purge it of dross; then throw in some sal ammoniac <note>original: "salis Ammonii"; ammonium chloride, used as a flux in metallurgy</note>; and with the fire increased so that the pot glows;

# CHAPTER XV.
## On the Calcination of Mars and Venus.

### Calcination of Mars.
<note>In alchemy, Mars refers to Iron or Steel.</note>

Carefully clean filings of steel from impurities by winnowing <note>blowing air through the filings to remove dust</note> and washing. Take two pounds of this and three pounds of prepared salt. Mix them together and heat in an earthen pot in a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" onto the material</note> for a natural day <note>a full 24-hour period</note>. Remove the mass and grind it; dissolve it in hot water and wash it repeatedly until it is freed from all saltiness and earthiness. It is then dried and reduced to a fine powder by grinding and sifting. Afterward, it is heated in the reverberatory furnace for eight or ten days, until the surface rises into a very red, impalpable <term>crocus</term> <note>Original: "crocum." Literally "saffron," a term used by early chemists for a fine, reddish powder, usually a metal oxide.</note>. Once this is removed, the remaining part is heated as many times and for as long until the whole amount turns into crocus. The earthen vessel containing the filings should have a lid, so that ashes do not fall onto the powder, yet it should be held high enough so that between the vessel and the lid, the flame has free passage.

# CHAPTER XVI.

## On the Calcination of Silver & Gold.

### Calcination of Silver.

**D**issolve Silver <note>original: "Lunam," or the Moon</note> in <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>nitric acid</note>: and by the pouring on of salty water, precipitate it to the bottom of the <term>matrass</term> <note>a long-necked glass flask</note> into a white powder <note>original: "calcem," literally "lime," referring to the metal reduced to a powder through chemical action</note>, which ought to be sweetened <note>original: "edulcorari," meaning to wash away the corrosive acids with water</note> by frequent pouring on of common water, and then dried. Of this powder, take one ounce. Of prepared salt: two ounces; of <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>: two drams. Mix these well in a glass mortar, and <term>reverberate</term> <note>apply intense heat in a furnace where the flames are "reflected" back onto the substance</note> for eight days. Afterward, a tincture is drawn out with <term>purified spirit of wine</term> <note>original: "spiritu vini alkolifato," or highly concentrated ethanol</note>, and it is <term>circulated</term> <note>the process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel</note>. It is beneficial for mania and other conditions of the brain.

### Calcination of Gold.

Make an amalgam of <term>Gold</term> <note>original: "Solis," or the Sun</note>, purified by <term>cementation</term> <note>a high-heat refining process using salts to remove impurities</note>, with six parts of <term>Mercury</term>, as follows. Take gold in thin plates, which you shall cut into tiny pieces with scissors: and place them in a clean crucible among living coals, so that the gold at least becomes red-hot. Then, from another small crucible, pour warmed <term>mercury</term> over the gold, and mix it with a small rod so that they are incorporated. Then throw it into cold water: and having washed the mass very well, pass it through leather, and squeeze out the superfluous mercury, so that a sufficiently hard mass remains,

# C H A P T E R XVI.
## *Diaphoretic <term>Thunder-Gold</term>.* <note>original: "Ceraunocryson Diaphoreticum." From the Greek words for "thunder" (keraunos) and "gold" (chrysos). This refers to fulminating gold, a chemically unstable and explosive compound.</note>

Dissolve the purest <term>sun</term> <note>In alchemical texts, the "Sun" (Sol) is the standard symbol for gold.</note> in <term>philosophical water</term> <note>original: "aqua philosophica," likely referring to aqua regia, a powerful mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids—the only substance known to the ancients that could dissolve gold.</note>, and digest it overnight in a sand bath. Then pour over it, drop by drop, <term>oil of Tartar</term> <note>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate.</note> until the bubbling ceases and the <term>calx</term> <note>a chemical precipitate or powder resulting from the process.</note> of gold is precipitated to the bottom of the vessel. This must be <term>sweetened</term> <note>original: "edulcorari," the process of washing a precipitate with water to remove any remaining acids or salts.</note> with many washings and dried over a very gentle fire. The dose is three or four grains.

And this <term>diaphoretic</term> <note>a medicine used to induce sweating, traditionally used to "break" a fever or expel toxins from the body.</note> can be prepared in an even more excellent way, in this manner: Take five or six grains of the Thunder-Gold and place them in a small silver vessel. Pour over it the best <term>rectified spirit of wine</term> <note>highly concentrated alcohol.</note>, ignite it, and suspend a crystal glass with a sufficiently wide opening above it. As soon as the spirit of wine has finished burning, the Thunder-Gold will <term>perform its function</term> <note>original: "officium suum faciet." This is a cautious way of describing the violent detonation of the gold fulminate, which happens when heat is applied.</note>, and a certain earthy part will be <term>sublimated</term> <note>the process where a solid turns into vapor and then deposits back into a solid on a cooler surface.</note> onto the walls of the glass. Repeat this four or five times, and wash the glass with spirit of wine so that the calx sinks to the bottom; this must then be dried. The dose is one or two grains.

# C H A P T E R XVII.

## On Salts.

***Method of extracting essential salt from herbs without <term>Calcination</term>.*** <note>original: "sine Calcinatione." Calcination involves burning a substance to ashes. Here, the author describes a method to get salt from a plant without destroying its "essential" qualities through fire.</note>

**T**ake a large quantity of <term>Blessed Thistle</term> <note>original: "carduus benedictus." A Mediterranean thistle widely used in the Renaissance as a "cure-all," especially for fevers and the plague.</note>: crush it in a stone or wooden mortar. Afterward, cook it in a large vessel with a great quantity of water until it is reduced by half. Then, strongly squeeze and strain it. Boil the strained liquid again until it reaches the thickness of liquid honey. This juice of Blessed Thistle should be placed in a glass vessel in a cold place for several days; it will generate an angular crystalline salt at the bottom of the vessel, in the manner of <term>rock salt</term> <note>original: "salis gemmæ." Naturally occurring crystalline salt (halite).</note>. Once the juice is poured off, the salt is collected, washed with Blessed Thistle water, and dried; keep this carefully. ### *Salt of Tartar.* <note>original: "Sal Tartari." Tartar is the potassium bitartrate crust that forms on the inside of wine barrels during fermentation; its "salt" (potassium carbonate) was a staple of early chemistry.</note>

Spread the Tartar in an unvitrified <note>original: "non vitreato." Meaning unglazed or porous.</note> earthen vessel with a flat bottom, to the thickness of a finger. It is then <term>reverberated</term> <note>original: "reverberatur." To be heated in a "reverberatory furnace" where the flames are reflected or "reverberated" off the roof onto the material.</note> until it reaches whiteness over the course of five or six hours, using a fire so moderated—to prevent melting—that the vessel merely glows. The Tartar, thus <term>calcined</term> <note>original: "calcinatum." Reduced to ash or powder through high heat.</note> to whiteness, is drenched in common water; it is <term>digested</term> <note>original: "digeritur." To be soaked in a liquid under gentle, steady heat to extract soluble components.</note>, filtered, and <term>coagulated</term> <note>original: "coagulatur." In this context, to boil away the liquid until only the solid salt remains.</note>.

### *Salt of Corals.* <note>original: "Sal Corallorum." Early modern physicians believed that the "salts" extracted from red coral possessed the concentrated life-force of the sea.</note>

This is made by <term>digesting</term> crushed corals in thrice-distilled vinegar overnight: then by filtering and evaporating the vinegar until dry. Thus, the salt of corals remains at the bottom of the vessel.

Its powers are excellent. For it purifies the blood throughout the entire body: it restores the original vigor of health: it stops <term>fluxes</term> <note>original: "fluxus." Any abnormal or excessive discharge of bodily fluids.</note> of the womb, the belly, and of hemorrhoids: it strengthens the heart and stomach, clears all obstructions of the internal organs, and dissolves clotted blood. It is also beneficial in <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "hydrope." Swelling caused by excess fluid in the tissues.</note>, convulsions, paralysis, <term>the stone</term> <note>original: "calculo." Kidney or bladder stones.</note>, and <term>suffocation of the womb</term> <note>original: "suffocatione matricis." A historical medical diagnosis where physical symptoms were attributed to the uterus "wandering" or "rising" in the body.</note>, if it is administered with a water appropriate to the specific ailment. The dose is from ten <term>grains</term> <note>A small unit of pharmaceutical weight, roughly 0.06 grams.</note> to one or two <term>scruples</term> <note>An apothecary weight equal to 20 grains, or about 1.3 grams.</note>, according to the age of the patient and the severity of the disease.

### *Salt of Colcothar.* <note>original: "Sal Colcotharis." Colcothar is the reddish-brown residue (iron oxide) left over after the distillation of vitriol, or sulfuric acid.</note>

# CHAPTER XIX.

## On Magisteries.

A **Magistery** <note>original: "Magisterium." In early chemistry, a magistery was a preparation where the entire substance was refined and "mastered" to a higher state without extracting specific oils or essences.</note> is when a composite body is prepared by the chymical art without extraction: so that all its homogeneous parts are preserved, raised to a nobler degree of either substance or quality, with the external impurities separated.

*Magistery of Tartar.*
Take four ounces of oil of Tartar <note>original: "olei Tartari." This is not a true oil, but a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate made by allowing the salt to liquefy in a moist cellar.</note> dissolved and purified from salt:
One ounce of Spirit of Vitriol <note>original: "Spiritus Vitrioli." A historical term for sulfuric acid.</note>:
Drop this drop by drop onto the oil of Tartar in a large glass: a very white coagulate will form. Let the moisture floating on top be drawn off with gentle heat, until the salt is dry: upon which distill <term>spirits of wine</term> <note>original: "vini spiritum." High-proof alcohol or ethanol.</note> three or four times: and thus you will have fixed white vitriolized Tartar.
Its use is for obstructions of all the internal organs: for stones: <term>nephritis</term> <note>original: "nephritide." Inflammation or disease of the kidneys.</note>: jaundice: retention of the menses: melancholy: hardness of the spleen: fevers: and <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "hydrope." Swelling caused by excess fluid in the body.</note>: if it is administered appropriately. The dose is from half a <term>scruple</term> <note>A unit of weight used by apothecaries, equal to 20 grains or about 1.3 grams.</note> to a whole one.

Dissolve ground corals or pearls in acidic water made with spirit of vitriol. Digest—

## Tartarized Spirit of Wine.

Distill dried wine dregs in the manner of "strong water" <note>original: "aquæ fortis." Usually refers to nitric acid, but here indicates the method of high-heat distillation.</note>. Separate and save the water and the oil. Meanwhile, calcine <note>To heat a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve decomposition or to burn off volatile parts.</note> the dregs until they are white, then soak them with the aforementioned oil. Distill and calcine again as before, repeating the work so many times until the oil becomes as clear as water and sweet, tasting of no burnt flavor. In this way, you will have the tartarized quintessence, which removes all corrosiveness from metals.

For the fourth time, slowly distill the phlegm <note>The watery, inactive portion of a distillate.</note>, and again pour on four new ounces [of the solvent]: proceed as before until all the water is consumed, and the entire "body" [of the gold] has been exalted and sublimated.

### CHAPTER I.
#### Concerning
#### *The fifth essence of human blood.*

The term **Fifth Essence** <note>original: "Quintæ Essentiæ." Also known as the Quintessence; in alchemy, this was considered the "hidden" fifth element beyond earth, air, fire, and water—the pure, medicinal soul of a substance.</note> has multiple meanings. Sometimes it signifies any chemical form stripped of the thickness of elemental matter and its bulky dregs; in this sense, it is contrasted with a <term>magistery</term> <note>original: "magisterio." A magistery is a preparation where the entire substance is purified and "exalted" as a whole, rather than being separated into its individual components (like oils or salts).</note>, in which almost the entire mass of the substance remains, though it is exalted and purified. At other times—and this is how we understand it here—it denotes an ethereal, celestial, and most subtle substance. This substance is brought together from the <term>three principles</term> <note>The "Tria Prima" of alchemy: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury. These were not the common materials we know today, but philosophical principles representing stability, flammability, and volatility.</note> of any dissolved compound body, once they have been stripped of their sensible, corruptible, and mortal elemental qualities through various chemical operations. It is then coagulated into one single thing: either a spiritual body or a corporeal spirit. It is called "fifth" from the fif- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "quin-" for "quinta" (fifth), to be continued on the next page.</note>

...called by some **Medicine Preeminent** <note>original Greek: "Κατ' ἐξοχὴν." Meaning the highest or most excellent form of medicine.</note>; by others it is called **Elixir**, on account of its remarkable virtues which it exerts in the preservation of the human body from various diseases. By others it is called **Heaven**, for a twofold reason. First, because just as heaven is not made from the four Elements, but from a certain ethereal matter and a sort of fifth element, and is not subject to any corruption: so also the true **Fifth Essence** is separated from all the dregs of the elements; and although it is not entirely incorruptible, it is nevertheless reduced to such subtlety, thinness, and spiritual simplicity that it seems to contain nothing heterogeneous <note>Meaning "of a different kind"; it contains no foreign substances that would cause it to spoil or decay.</note> within itself by which it could be corrupted. Secondly, because just as heaven acts powerfully upon these sublunary things <note>The "sublunary" realm refers to the Earth and everything below the moon, which was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the unchanging heavens.</note>, granting and conserving life to all things: so also this Fifth Essence conserves the health of the human body, extends youth, delays old age, and drives away every kind of disease.

Furthermore, the Fifth Essence of human blood is prepared in this manner: Take a sufficiently large quantity of the blood of healthy men, established in the flower of their age; place it in a circulatory vessel <note>A "circulatory vessel" or Pelican was a glass flask with arms that allowed distilled vapors to condense and flow back into the base, cycling the substance continuously.</note> of the proper capacity in a <term>B. M.</term> <note>original: "Balneum Mariae" or Mary's Bath. A water bath used to provide gentle, consistent heat.</note>, boiling continuously until the **Dragon** <note>original: "Draco." A reference to the Ouroboros, the serpent eating its own tail. In alchemical practice, this symbolizes the completion of the "circulation" process, where the substance has been refined by its own vapors.</note> has devoured its own tail. When the vessels have cooled, take out the material, which will be like liver, and cut it into small pieces; and through high cucurbits <note>The lower part of a distilling apparatus, named for its gourd-like shape.</note>, with the same heat of the bath, separate the watery element or <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "phlegma." In early chemistry, this refers to the watery, tasteless, and medically inactive part of a substance separated during distillation.</note> by distillation.

A portion of this should be set aside separately to serve as a solvent.

# CHAPTER II.
## Concerning the quintessence of wine.

**P**lace a noble wine for one month in a <term>horse’s belly: a pile of fermenting horse manure used as a source of gentle, consistent heat</term> or its substitute, in circulating vessels of suitable size. Afterward, distill the spirit in a <term>B. M.</term> <note>original: "Balneum Mariae" or Mary's Bath; a water bath used for gentle heating</note> in tall gourd-shaped vessels <note>original: "cucurbitis"</note>; when this has been rectified four times, separating the <term>phlegm: the watery, inactive part of a distilled liquid</term> at each turn, distill it yet seven more times: so that out of forty pounds of wine, you separate one pound of the most spiritual part (for that which is distilled between the spirit and the phlegm is <term>burning water: high-proof alcohol or "aqua ardens"</term>). Keep the Spirit in a glass vessel, half-filled and properly sealed, so that it does not breathe out <note>i.e., evaporate</note>.

### *On the quintessence of Corals.*

**F**irst, a large quantity of very sharp vinegar must be distilled, with the separation of the <term>Phlegm: the watery, tasteless, and medically inactive portion of a distillate</term> which is useless for this work, distilling new vinegar each time over the previous dregs, until you have about a hundred pounds of vinegar optimally <term>rectified: purified and strengthened through repeated distillation</term> by a <term>B.: Balneum Mariae, or water bath</term>. This refers to the vigorous effervescence caused by the acid in the vinegar reacting with the calcium carbonate in the coral.</note>, until it stands four or five finger-widths above the powder; and digesting it for a natural day <note>A "natural day" refers to a full 24-hour cycle.</note> in the water bath, until the vinegar becomes sweet and is imbued with a yellow color. Then the <term>menstruum: a solvent used to extract the "essence" of a substance</term> must be poured off and new solvent poured back on, until everything that can be dissolved has been dissolved. The solvent should be processed again by the water bath using tall <term>cucurbits: the bottom part of a distilling apparatus, shaped like a gourd</term>; and for each pound of salt <note>In alchemy, "salt" often refers to the solid crystalline residue remaining after a liquid has been evaporated or distilled.</note>, two ounces of vinegar should be poured on and distilled; then four ounces are added, then six; thus nourishing the substance gradually and in stages, and finally decreasing the infusions ounce by ounce, until the vinegar is distilled just as sharp as it was when it was first put in. # TREATISE
## T H E  F I R S T.

*Concerning Nature: what it is, and what kind of searchers it ought to have.*

**M**any wise and most learned men, many centuries ago—indeed, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure considered the father of alchemy and the "Hermetic" tradition.</note> testifies, even before the flood—wrote many things concerning the preparation of the <term>Philosophers' Stone</term> <note>original: "lapide Philosophorum"; the legendary substance believed to be capable of transmuting base metals into gold and curing all diseases.</note> and left us so many writings that, unless <term>Nature</term> <note>original: "Natura"; personified here as the guiding force of the physical world.</note> performed credible works for us daily, hardly anyone would now believe Nature to be true. This is because in previous ages there were not so many "inventors" of things; nor did our predecessors consider anything else besides Nature itself and the possibility of Nature. And although they remained only in the simple path of Nature, they nevertheless discovered those things which we, now occupied with so many matters, could hardly have imagined with our own wits. This happens because to us, Nature and the generation of things in the world now seem common and simple; and for that reason, we direct our wits not toward known things, but toward such things as cannot—or can hardly—be done. Wherefore it so happens to us that it is easier to devise subtle things, and things which the Philosophers themselves did not know, to ima-

Know, however, that the limit of Nature is God, who is also the beginning of Nature; for no beginning is ended except in that in which it begins. # FOURTH
## TREATISE.

### *How metals are generated in the bowels of the earth.*

**M**etals are produced in this way: after the four Elements cast their virtues into the center of the earth, the <term>Archæus</term> <note>The internal "master craftsman" or vital spirit that directs the processes of nature, a central concept in Paracelsian alchemy</note>, by distilling through the heat of perpetual motion, sublimates them toward the surface of the earth. For the earth is porous, and the wind, by distilling through the pores of the earth, is resolved into water, from which all things are born. Therefore, let the sons of doctrine <note>A traditional term for students or initiates of the alchemical arts</note> know that the sperm of metals is no different from the sperm of all things: namely, a <term>moist vapor</term> <note>original: "vaporem humidum"</note>. For this reason, Artists <note>Alchemists practicing the laboratory arts</note> seek in vain the reduction of metals into <term>first matter</term> <note>original: "materiam primam"; the primordial, formless substance of the universe</note>, which is nothing but vapor. The Philosophers did not mean such a first matter, but only the <term>second matter</term> <note>original: "materiam secundam"; the specific substance that has already begun to take on the characteristics of a metal</note>, as **Bernard of Treviso** <note>Bernardus Trevisanus (1406–1490), an influential alchemist whose writings emphasized the natural, slow growth of metals within the earth</note> most excellently argues—though not so clearly, because he speaks of the four Elements. Nevertheless, this is what he intended to say, and he spoke only to the "sons." I, however, so that I might more clearly reveal the **Theory**, have wished here to caution and warn everyone to abandon so many solutions, so many circulations, so many calcinations <note>Common alchemical laboratory processes: dissolving substances, recycling vapors in a closed vessel, and heating solids to a powder</note> and reiterations; for in vain is that...

But **Metals** <note>original: "Metalla"</note> are procreated in this way: the earth is purified by a long distillation; afterwards they are generated by the arrival of <term>fatness</term> <note>original: "pinguedinis"; an alchemical term for the oily, sulfurous principle that gives body and "fuel" to metals</note>; they do not arise in any other way, despite the vain opinion of those who incorrectly interpret the writings of certain Philosophers.

As for how colors are formed in gemstones, it should be known that this happens by means of **sulfur** in the following manner: if the fatness of the sulfur is congealed by that perpetual motion <note>referring to the constant circulation of vapors within the earth's crust</note>, the vital spirit of the water, in passing through, afterwards "digests" <note>a term for slow, gentle heating that matures or "ripens" a substance</note> and purifies it, until it is colored with a matured red or white hue. For all water is congealed by heat if it lacks the spirit, but is congealed by cold if it contains the spirit. However, the one who knows how to congeal water through heat and join the spirit with it will surely find something a thousand times more precious than gold or any other thing. 

Therefore, let the seeker ensure that the spirit is separated from the water, so that it may undergo <term>putrefaction</term> <note>original: "putrescat"; the stage of breaking down or "rotting" a substance to release its inner essence</note> and the "grain" may appear. Then, having cast aside the dregs, let him lead the spirit back from on high into the water and cause them to be joined together; for that union will generate a "branch" <note>a new substance or alchemical growth</note> that is unlike its parents in form.
