**W**E have spoken of the <term>first matter</term> <note>original: "prima materia"; the primal, formless substance from which all things are fundamentally made</note> of things, and how things are born from Nature without seed—that is, how Nature receives from the Elements the matter from which it generates the seed. The **seed**, therefore, as has already been repeated many times, is an invisible thing, but the **sperm** is visible, and is almost a living soul; it is not found in dead things. This **intrinsic heat** is much more effective than this **elemental fire** <note>elemental fire: the common fire used in kitchens or furnaces, which was considered less pure and powerful than the internal heat of nature</note>, but it is tempered by earthly water, which from day to day penetrates the pores of the earth and cools it. <meta>Catchword: water</meta>

...rate, without the mediation of air. But how these elements act among themselves, I shall say in brief. In the center of the earth is a **Central Sun**, which by its own motion, or that of its firmament, gives off a great heat that extends itself all the way to the surface of the earth. That heat produces air in this manner: the **matrix** <note>The "matrix" refers to a womb or originating source from which a substance is generated.</note> of air is water, which gives birth to children of its own nature, but unlike itself and much more subtle. For where there is an entrance for water, air is shut out; it enters when, afterward, that central heat—which is perpetual—acts upon it. It causes the water to distill and grow warm, and thus that water, by the power of the heat, is turned into air. In this way, it bursts forth to the surface of the earth because it does not allow itself to be enclosed. There, after it has cooled, it is resolved back into water in the appropriate places. 

Sometimes it also happens that not only air but even water goes out, just as it appears when black clouds are raised into the air with violence. Let this domestic example serve you for this matter: if you were to boil water in a **pot** <note>original: "ollâ"</note>, you would see that with a more vehement fire, thicker mists will appear. In exactly the same way, the central heat works: it elevates subtle water into air, while that which is thick—derived from salt or **fatness** <note>In alchemy, "fatness" (pinguedine) refers to a fertile, oily, or combustible principle within matter, rather than literal fat.</note>—it distributes to the earth, from which various things are born; the remainder becomes rocks and stones. Someone might object that if the matter were so, then it ought to happen continuously, yet often no wind is felt. I respond: if water is not poured violently into a **distillation vessel** <note>original: "vas destillatoriū"</note>, no wind is produced, for a little water...

# T R E A T I S E
## T W E L F T H.

### *Concerning the stone and its virtue.*

**I**n the preceding sections, enough has been said regarding the production of natural things, the <term>Elements</term> <note>In alchemical theory, the four elements—Earth, Air, Fire, and Water—are the fundamental building blocks of all matter, driven by internal heat.</note>, fertile matter, bodies and seeds, and their use and power. As they are worthy of trust in their own art, their credibility should not be dismissed. ...of the Creator? Shall we exclude [metals] from the universal blessing of multiplication, which the Holy Scriptures <note>Referencing the command in Genesis to "be fruitful and multiply."</note> affirm was granted and imparted to all created things immediately from the foundation of the world? Truly, if they possess seed, who is so foolish as not to believe that they can be multiplied in their own seed? In its nature, the art of <term>Chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chymiæ". In this era, "Chemistry" and "Alchemy" were used interchangeably to describe the study of the transformation of matter.</note> is true, and nature is true, but rarely is the craftsman true. There is one nature, one art, but many craftsmen. 

Now, whereas nature creates things from the elements, she generates them by the will of God out of <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: "materia prima". The fundamental, formless substance from which all material things are created, according to Aristotelian and alchemical philosophy.</note>, which God alone knows. Nature creates those things and multiplies them from the secondary matter, which the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Philosophi". Not academic philosophers, but the "Sages" or master alchemists who understand the hidden laws of nature.</note> know. Nothing happens in the world without the will of God and of nature. 

For every element is in its own sphere, but one cannot exist without the other; one lives from the other, and yet when joined they do not harmonize. But water is the most worthy of all elements, because it is the mother of all things. Over this floats the <term>spirit of fire</term> <note>original: "spiritus ignis". A vital, animating heat that the author likely correlates with the Spirit of God moving over the waters in Genesis.</note>. By the action of fire, water becomes the <term>prime matter</term>—namely, through the struggle of fire with water—and thus winds or suitable vapors are generated, to be congealed with earth by means of the raw air which was separated from it from the beginning. 

And this happens without ceasing, by <term>perpetual motion</term> <note>original: "motu perpetuo". The author describes a cyclical, self-sustaining natural process rather than a mechanical device.</note>, because fire or heat is not excited otherwise than by motion. This is easily seen in the case of a blacksmith crushing iron with a file; the iron grows hot by the more vehement motion, just as if it had been made red-hot in a fire.

[...they] have recognized how nature produces things by her operation, so that they might not enter the gate without keys, or draw water with a sieve; for he labors in vain who stretches out his hands to work without the knowledge of nature. But when the clothes are removed and they are stripped bare, so that they appear as nature formed them, each is easily distinguished by their sex. It was not my intention to publish this book, for the reasons mentioned in the preface; however, the desire to be of service to noble and Philosophical minds overcame me. I wished to show my good will to those who know me, and at the same time, to manifest to those who are skilled in the art that I am their equal and companion, seeking their acquaintance. 

I do not doubt that many men of good conscience and will secretly possess that gift of God. Let these men, warned by my example and made more cautious and provident by the dangers I have faced, keep for themselves the <term>silence of Harpocrates</term> <note>original: "Harpocratis silentium." # BY THE SAME AUTHOR
## TO THE SONS OF TRUTH.

### *A Philosophical Enigma.*

Now, you <term>sons of science</term> <note>original: "filii scientiæ." A traditional address to dedicated students of alchemy, implying they are the intellectual heirs to this secret knowledge.</note>, I have revealed everything to you from the <term>source of the universal fountain</term> <note>original: "è scaturigine universalis fontis." For in my preceding Treatises, I have sufficiently explained nature through examples; I have manifested the theory and practice as much as was divinely permitted. But lest anyone should complain of <term>brevity</term> <note>original: "Laconismo." Named after the Spartans of Laconia, who were famous for their concise, pithy way of speaking. There are infinite books treating this art, yet in hardly any of them will you find the truth revealed to this extent. I wished to provide this because I have conversed with many who thought they understood the writings of the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Philosophorum." I asked: "Is it useful without this fruit of the **Tree**?" To this he said: "In this work, not at all, since it is improved only in this fruit of the **Solar Tree** alone."

## TO THE KIND READER.

**Q**uince your inquiry, *friend Reader*, as to who the author of this *little treatise* <note>original: "Tractatuli." The use of the diminutive suggests a modest or brief work.</note> might be: but as for why he wrote it, let this be the reason. It is also not necessary for you to know who I am: however, know for a most certain certainty that the *Author* of this little work has successfully brought forth, holds, and possesses the PHILOSOPHERS' STONE <term>Philosophers' Stone (Lapis Philosophorum): The legendary substance of alchemy capable of transmuting base metals into gold and acting as a universal medicine.</term> in its most perfect state. Since we regard one another with mutual and sincere kindness, I requested that, as a sign of his affection for me, he discuss the three first principles—namely, MERCURY, SULPHUR, and SALT <note>Known as the "Tria Prima," these were the three fundamental components of matter in Paracelsian alchemy, representing spirit, soul, and body.</note>—and that he might indicate whether the PHILOSOPHERS' STONE should be sought in these common things or in others. I asked that he do this in the simplest words and the plainest style. After he had granted my wish by quickly writing this little treatise, I became fully persuaded that by publishing it—even though I fear it may be less pleasing to the *Author* (for all ambition is far from him)—lovers of true Philosophy would be most grateful to me. For I have no doubt that, once it is read and well considered, they will suffer less loss, expense, and damage from impostors, and less waste of time, reputation, and honor. If I find the honest world (for I hate and keep away the profane rabble of *Alchemists* <note>The writer makes a common distinction between "true philosophers" and the "puffers" or fraudulent alchemists who sought only material wealth through trickery.</note>) to be grateful for this kind intention of mine, I shall strive to see that the remaining two principles and many other things from the same *Author* follow. In the meantime, enjoy this and farewell.

<summary>A preface written by a friend of the author, introducing a short treatise on the three principles of alchemy (Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt). The writer explains that he is publishing the work to protect honest students from the financial and moral ruin caused by alchemical frauds.</summary>

You are the Philosopher, I am the Servant of Philosophers; what they wish to make from me, they make; I obey them as much as I am able. *Alchemist:* You ought to tell me how I should proceed with you, and if I can make the **Philosophical Stone** from you. *Mercury:* If you know, you will do it; if indeed you do not know, you will do nothing: you will learn nothing from me if you do not know beforehand, my Lord Philosopher. *Alchemist:* You speak with me as if with some simple man; perhaps you are unaware that I have worked for great Princes, and was a philosopher among them. *Mercury:* I easily believe it, my Lord, for I know those things very well; I am still filthy from the mixture of that labor. <note>Mercury is likely referring to the physical "mess" of improper chemical experiments, while also mocking the Alchemist's "distinguished" past as mere soot and grime.</note> *Alchemist:* Tell me then, are You the **Mercury of the Philosophers**? <term>Mercury of the Philosophers</term> <note>In alchemy, this refers not to common quicksilver (liquid mercury metal), but to the "essential" or "living" spirit of the metal required for the Great Work.</note> *Mercury:* I am Mercury; but whether I am the one belonging to the Philosophers, you ought to know. *Alchemist:* Tell me only if you are the true Mercury, or if there is another? *Mercury:* I am Mercury, but there is also another—and with that, he vanished. The Alchemist shouts and speaks, but no one answers him. And thinking to himself he says: "Truly I am a most excellent man; [Mercury] has spoken with me..."

"Mercury certainly loves me," the Alchemist said, and he began to work diligently once again. ...now you mix me with almost all the most filthy things and with dung.

*Mercury:* You sow me in dung, and at the time of the harvest, I vanish, but you are accustomed to reaping only dung.

*Alchemist:* Yet the Philosophers wrote thus: that their "matter" ought to be sought in a dunghill <note>In alchemical literature, the "dunghill" (Latin: *sterquilinium*) was a common metaphor for a lowly, discarded, or common substance that actually contained the "seed" of gold.</note>.

Mercury is mocking the Alchemist for following the words of books exactly without understanding the hidden, allegorical meaning intended by the authors.</note>, and not their true sense and mind.

*Alchemist:* Now I see that perhaps you are Mercury; but you do not wish to obey me. 

And he began to conjure him again, saying: **U x, U x** <note>These appear to be magical syllables or a phonetic incantation used in an attempt to bind or command the spirit of Mercury.</note>. But Mercury, laughing, replied: You will accomplish nothing, my friend.

*Alchemist:* Not in vain do they say of you that you are wonderful, and inconstant, and volatile.

*Mercury:* You say that I am inconstant; I will explain <note>original: "sic solvo," literally "I solve it thus."</note> this to you in this way. I am constant to a constant craftsman, and fixed to a fixed mind; but you and your kind are the inconstant ones, wandering from one thing to another, and from one material to another.

*Alchemist:* Tell me then, if you are that Mercury of whom the Philosophers wrote—whom they called, along with **sulfur** and **salt**, the principle of all things <term>The Three Principles</term> <note>Also known as the *Tria Prima*, these were the three fundamental substances (Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt) that alchemists believed made up all material bodies.</note>—or is another to be sought?

*Mercury:* Certainly the fruit does not fall far from the tree, but I do not seek my own glory: I am the same as I was, but my years are different. From the beginning I was young as long as I was alone. But now I am older, yet still the same as I was.

->### DIALOGUE <-

...is a gem. Although it was only one, it is nothing, and its number is whole. In it are the four **Elements** <term>Elements: The four building blocks of the universe—Earth, Air, Fire, and Water—which alchemists believed must be balanced to create the Stone</term>, yet it is not an **Element**. It is a poison, and yet it cures leprosy <note>original: "lepram" — in alchemy, "leprosy" refers to the impurities or "corrosion" found in base metals, which the Stone is said to "heal" by transforming them into gold</note>; it is life, and yet it kills all things. It is a King, yet another possesses his kingdom; it flees with fire, and yet fire is prepared from it; it is water and does not wet; it is earth, and yet it is sown; it is air, and yet it lives by water.

***Alchemist:*** Now I see that I know nothing, but I do not dare to say so; for I would lose my good reputation, and my neighbor would no longer invest in me <note>literally "spend on me"</note> if he knew that I know nothing. I will, however, say that I know for certain, otherwise no one would even give me bread; for many of them hope for many good things from me.

***Nature:*** Even if you drag this out for a long time, what will be the result? In the meantime, any of your neighbors will demand their expenses back from you.

***Alchemist:*** I will feed everyone I can with hope.

***Nature:*** And what then, in the end?

***Alchemist:*** I will quietly attempt various works; if it succeeds, I will pay them back. If not, I will go to another province and cultivate the same thing there.

***Nature:*** And what will happen after that?

***Alchemist:*** Ha, ha, ha! There are many provinces, and many greedy men as well, to whom I will promise a great abundance of gold, and in the shortest time too. And so, day will follow day; meanwhile, either the King [dies], or the don- <note>original: "asi-" — the catchword "nus" on the bottom of the page indicates the word "asinus" or "donkey." This likely refers to the proverb "either the King will die or the donkey will die," meaning the fraudster is just stalling for time until circumstances change.</note>

<summary>Nature provides a series of alchemical paradoxes describing the Prime Matter, leading the Alchemist to confess that he is a charlatan who exploits the greed of others to survive.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury, Philosopher's Stone, Four Elements, alchemical paradoxes, fraud, greed, Prime Matter</keywords>

<page-num>379</page-num>
->### MERCURY'S [DIALOGUE] <-

...either he will die, or I.

**Nature.** A noose (rightfully) awaits such **Philosophers**: depart, and put an end to yourself and to such philosophy of yours, on an evil cross <note>original: "malâ cruce" — a common Latin idiom or curse used to wish someone a wretched or shameful end, often translated as "go and be hanged"</note>, as quickly as possible; for by this single counsel, you will be a fraud neither to me, nor to your neighbor <note>In alchemical texts, "neighbor" or "proximum" often refers to the patrons or fellow citizens who funded the Alchemist's expensive and often fruitless experiments</note>, nor even to yourself.

## THE END
